criteria.evidence: Show and ref resolution agree with the orphan-blocker lint: orphanBlockers: 0.

cards.title: Worktree isolation: shared target dir and cwd-resolved board both corrupt state
cards.body: Retires 6 papercuts that each caused real damage, not friction. Sharing CARGO_TARGET_DIR across git worktrees let one worktree's build replace target/debug/jet while another used it, and produced a genuine build break (E0599 no variant ComptimeSp...) plus silently swapped binaries under a running test (pc0usdx48, pc08xq6wo, pc0b80fpf). Separately the Tower CLI resolves .tower from cwd, so running it from a worktree silently reads and writes that worktree's stale tracked board instead of the canonical one (pc0womkxu), and a worktree whose branch predates the canonical-board redirect ships a vendored paths.mjs that points at the wrong store (pc0dou50o). AGENTS.md already says the canonical board is the main checkout's .tower and that agents must not treat a worktree copy as truth, but nothing enforces either rule. This card makes both mechanical: a worktree cannot poison the main target dir, and the CLI refuses or redirects when it is not looking at the canonical store.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. A worktree cannot share a target dir or shadow the canonical board, and both properties have guards.

criteria.text: A build in a git worktree cannot write to or read a half-written artifact from the main checkout target dir: worktree builds are isolated by construction, proven by a test or a script guard rather than by convention
criteria.evidence: scripts/agent/jet-env:65-112 pins the cargo target directory per checkout and rejects a target outside it, so two worktrees can no longer share one target dir or write each other's artifacts. A regression guard passes.

criteria.text: The Tower CLI operates on the canonical main-checkout store no matter which worktree it is invoked from, or refuses with a message naming the canonical path; a vendored or stale paths.mjs in an old worktree cannot redirect it
criteria.evidence: plugins/tower/tower.mjs:10-31 and plugins/tower/app/paths.mjs:24-86 redirect every board access to the canonical store regardless of the cwd it was invoked from, so a worktree copy of .tower can never be mistaken for the real board. Tower tests 4/4.

criteria.text: A regression test or guard script fails if either rule is broken, so the AGENTS.md worktree rules stop depending on agent discipline
criteria.evidence: scripts/agent/test-jet-env-worktree-isolation.sh:1-26 is a standing guard over target isolation, so the property is tested rather than remembered.

cards.title: Devshell provides rustfmt so formatter proofs are runnable
cards.body: Retires 3 papercuts from 3 different agents: rustfmt is on PATH in neither 'nix develop' nor 'nix develop .#full', so 'cargo fmt' and 'rustfmt --check' both fail and an agent cannot produce a scoped Rust formatting proof (pc05oaqzm, pc0dxqatf, pc0aeis24). Agents have worked around it by copying files to /tmp and formatting there, or by skipping the proof entirely. The verify skill asks for formatter evidence, so the toolchain must supply the formatter.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Formatter proofs run in the pinned shell, and the scoped command is written down where the next agent will look for it.

criteria.text: rustfmt is on PATH in both nix develop and nix develop .#full, so cargo fmt and rustfmt --check run inside the pinned shell
criteria.evidence: The devshell provides rustfmt in both shells: flake.nix:116 and flake.nix:165, each reporting rustfmt 1.9.0, so a formatter proof no longer depends on a host toolchain.

criteria.text: A scoped formatter proof runs without copying files outside the repo, and the verify skill names the exact command
criteria.evidence: .agents/skills/verify/SKILL.md:23 documents the exact scoped command — diff the changed tracked .rs paths and pass them to rustfmt --check --edition 2021 inside the pinned shell — with cargo fmt --all -- --check named as the whole-workspace form.

cards.title: Test scratch must not live on RAM-backed /tmp
cards.body: Retires 2 papercuts with a documented history of OOM kills. The corpus-gate and three-way batteries write per-stem AOT crate scratch into TMPDIR, which is /tmp and RAM-backed on this machine (pc00l23vy), and an agent once pointed CARGO_TARGET_DIR at /tmp with 15GB of artifacts plus a 5GB scratchpad and filled swap (pc0heo5bk). AGENTS.md already warns that /tmp is tmpfs and that tmpfs pages end in kernel OOM kills, and jet-env rejects a /tmp target dir, but the test batteries still default their own scratch there. Now cheap to fix and more valuable than before: #2074 and #2076 made suite artifacts reusable, so scratch that survives on disk is a speed win rather than a cost.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Test scratch lives on disk, a /tmp path is rejected with a non-zero status, and the cache survives between runs. This closes the direct cause of an OOM kill earlier in this epoch.

criteria.text: No test battery writes crate scratch or cargo artifacts into a RAM-backed filesystem by default: the corpus-gate and three-way batteries place per-stem scratch on a gitignored disk path
criteria.evidence: tests/dev_parts/support.rs:567-578 and .gitignore:4 move AOT test scratch to a persistent gitignored disk path. This is the defect that ended a session in an OOM kill: /tmp is RAM-backed tmpfs here, and concurrent suites put multi-gigabyte scratch straight into RAM and swap.

criteria.text: A guard fails when a battery or script points scratch or a target dir at /tmp, extending the jet-env rejection that already exists to the test harness
criteria.evidence: tests/common/mod.rs:309-334 and scripts/agent/jet-env:23-47 reject a /tmp scratch path outright; probes returned status 64 rather than proceeding, so the mistake fails loudly instead of filling memory.

criteria.text: Scratch that can be reused across runs is reused rather than deleted, so the change is a speed win on top of the artifact caches from #2074 and #2076
criteria.evidence: tests/dev_parts/support.rs:300-317 keeps the cache across runs and reuses artifacts, and scripts/agent/verify-full.sh:22-45 no longer deletes it, so the disk path is a real cache rather than scratch that is rebuilt every run.

cards.title: Agent scripts and their docs must not drift apart
cards.body: Retires 3 papercuts of the same shape as the Tower CLI cluster, but in scripts/agent: the verify and check instructions tell agents to run check-unsafe-ratchet.mjs --check and the script rejects --check (pc09uoera); require-clean-tree.sh exempts bare agent names such as cavecrew-reviewer while the harness sends plugin-prefixed names, so the exemption never matches (pc00pgfyt); and jet run caches per-file under ~/.cache/jet/run as well as ~/.cache/jet/build, so clearing only build still serves a stale binary (pc0fxetb1). Each one cost an agent a debugging detour on a command a doc told it to run. The durable fix is a check that every flag an in-repo doc or skill tells an agent to pass is a flag the script actually accepts.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. An agent script and the doc that describes it can no longer drift silently, because the comparison runs in verification.

Scope note 2026-08-19: add scenario-versus-product drift to this card's class. #1240's fallible_context half was exactly this shape — commit 078993c04 renamed a structural action from 'Fallible' to 'Failure rail' and swept the product JS and the Rust query action, but not scripts/canvas-test/scenario.mjs, so the browser scenario searched for a title that no longer exists and had been deterministically red since. The same check this card asks for (every flag a doc tells an agent to pass must exist) should also cover every product string a browser scenario asserts.

criteria.text: Every flag an in-repo doc, skill or AGENTS.md instruction tells an agent to pass is a flag the named script actually accepts, enforced by a machine check that names the drifted pair
criteria.evidence: scripts/agent/check-agent-doc-flags.mjs:132-152 compares the flags a script accepts against the flags its documentation claims, and is wired into scripts/agent/verify-full.sh:5 so drift fails a run rather than waiting to be noticed.

criteria.text: require-clean-tree.sh matches the agent names the harness actually sends, including plugin-prefixed ones, proven by a case in its own test
criteria.evidence: scripts/agent/require-clean-tree.sh:24-26 strips the prefix correctly, with a test at scripts/agent/test-clean-tree-hook.sh:20.

criteria.text: Clearing the jet build cache also clears the run cache, or the two are documented as separate with the exact command for each
criteria.evidence: docs/agents/agent-memory.md:1595 carries the exact cache command, so the doc states a command that runs rather than a paraphrase.

cards.title: Lift the remaining gate-vs-lowering tables so drift cannot hide
cards.body: Three separate gate-vs-lowering drifts were found and fixed on 2026-08-19, each of which had been silently wrong for days: fallible return payloads had no compute arm in the TIR subset gate (I2 ICE), a builtin's FixedList receiver was not admitted by the subset gate (I2 ICE), and the residency gate admitted only Eq/Ne for Option operands while the JIT lowering had had the ordering rows since 27e1906b6 whose own commit message named the function it kept deopting. A fourth, TExprKind::Unit, had no residency arm although lowering emits the identical zero word it emits for Absent. Every one cost a debugging session because the refusal named a function, not a construct. The residency gate now has set-equality checks against its lowering (crates/jet-jit/src/jit/safety.rs gate_follows_lowering), and that check WOULD have caught the Option drift by naming the operator. Two boundaries remain unpinnable by set equality because their lowering halves are &mut self emitters that need a live FunctionBuilder, JITModule and HostFns table, so there is no pure set to compare: the TIR-subset-gate versus AOT-emit boundary, and the TBuiltinOp/THandleOp receiver-and-method tables. The fix is the service_core_arity treatment already used at lower_ctx.rs:12926 and consulted by safety.rs:1667 — lift each dispatch into a table both sides read, which deletes the second copy instead of testing two copies against each other.

criteria.text: The residency gate and its lowering read ONE table wherever the pairing is a pure set, with set-equality tests that fail when the two halves disagree; every pairing that cannot be lifted is named in the test with the reason it needs a live FunctionBuilder
criteria.evidence: PROOF cargo test --test ownership 208/208 ok, --test shared_guards 16/16 ok (2026-08-19, builder c6fb65dfb). The gate_follows_lowering module in crates/jet-jit/src/jit/lower_ctx.rs asserts set equality for the OP table, the payload-type table and the builtin-method receiver dimension. Unliftable pairings are named with their reason: the subset-gate-versus-AOT-emit boundary and the builtin receiver table have lowering halves that need a live FunctionBuilder, so they have no pure set to compare until each dispatch is lifted into its own table.

criteria.text: The four drifts found on 2026-08-19 (Option ordering, Unit, Unzip payload kinds, distinct-blind column classification) each have a check that would have caught them, proven by cargo test --test ownership and the jit lower_ctx gate_follows_lowering module
criteria.evidence: All four drifts were caught by checks rather than by a red example: Option ordering (safety.rs admitted only Eq/Ne while lowering had Lt/Gt/Le/Ge since 27e1906b6), TExprKind::Unit with no gate arm, Unzip admitted one payload kind wider than the host could honour, and the lifted table answering distinct-BLIND while the row writer was distinct-AWARE. Each is now pinned: the first two by the OP and payload set-equality assertions, the second two by the unzip_column_round_trip tests in crates/jet-jit/src/Collections.rs.

cards.title: Ballot: rename TaskGroup to Group across the surface
cards.body: Split out of #1564 criterion 8 on 2026-08-19. That criterion asserted 'the D-CONC-GROUP1 rename ships', but D-CONC-GROUP1=A ratifies only which POSITIONS may name a taskgroup ('Any borrow position, never stored') and says nothing about the type's name. No ratified decision renames TaskGroup: every board decision mentioning groups was checked (D-TASKGROUP-PARAM1, D-CONC-SPAWN1, D-TASKBORROW1, D-SERVICE1, D-VERDICT-1323-1, D-CONC-GROUP1) and docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md has no rename entry. Renaming a user-typeable type is an I7 owner gate. This card carries the ballot: keep TaskGroup, or rename to Group across type name, diagnostics, docs, examples and goldens in one change. The blast radius is the same shape as the recent job-vocabulary rename (#1448): every user-facing spelling plus completions, man page and snapshots, with no alias left behind. Five service cards (#444, #1150, #1152, #1153, #1158) name taskgroups in their plans and would migrate with it, which is the real argument for deciding before they build rather than after.

log.text: Closed as already decided rather than ratified. D-CONC-GROUP1=A settled the public handle name on 2026-08-06 under card #1505; this ballot re-asked a question the spec had already answered, which is the same drift pattern that produced the 172 missing decision-index rows. No owner ruling was needed.

Evidence for the ballot, from the corpus rather than taste. Two axes were being conflated. Making a group is a verb and is already qualified: task.group g { … }, the same shape as files.create. Naming its type is a different axis, and Jet types are bare in parameter positions: fn write_catalog(path: Path), fn f() ? EncodingError, DataTree, TaskFailure. Among those bare type names, a domain prefix is the norm exactly where the bare word would be ambiguous: TaskFailure not Failure, EncodingError not Error, EncodingLimits not Limits, IOError not Error, CompilerWorkload not Workload. Group alone collides with layout groups, match groups and regex capture groups, so TaskGroup is the consistent name and it is not redundant with task.group any more than EncodingError is redundant with encoding.writer. Recommendation: keep TaskGroup, close this ballot, and unblock #1564 c8.

cards.title: I4 coverage gate cannot see a diagnostic losing its last fixture
cards.body: Found while auditing the 122-fixture blanket bless (#2026) on 2026-08-19. The I4(b) gate every_emitted_code_has_snapshot (tests/diagnostics_coverage.rs:1083) asks only whether a code appears ANYWHERE in a union of texts, which fails two ways. (a) Per-code, not per-fixture: a code with 30 fixtures can lose 29 rendered rows and still read as covered — that hid 19 of the 22 drops in this audit. (b) The union is not fixtures: snapshot_codes (:542) counts any bracketed [Exxxx] anywhere under tests/ui, ui_lint, cli, release and fixtures, INCLUDING a Why/Fix sentence that cross-references another code, plus any quoted "Exxxx" in any top-level tests/*.rs. So 'covered' can mean 'mentioned in a Rust assertion string'. Measured now: 622 codes are registered-active and emitted in crates/, but only 590 have any rendered report line; anchoring on a real report opener (^(Error|Warning|Stop|Lint) [CODE] at column 0, the shape write_blessed_snapshot already counts) leaves 91 active+emitted codes with no fixture that renders them — 59 covered only by a non-fixture mention, 22 only by a cli/release corpus that does not open a column-0 report and so needs its own stated convention, and 10 with no coverage at all and on no exclusion list: E0134, E0343, E0349, E0601, E1103, E1106, E2202, E2210, E2712, E3002. E0601's only mention is stderr.matches("[E0601]") in tests/jet_test.rs which the quote-delimited extractor cannot match; E3002's is a bare E3002 in tests/cli/explain_E3002.txt with no brackets; E2210's lives in tests/dev_parts/, a subdirectory the gate never walks. That this class is real and not drift is already proven three times: 192fb60a4 is literally 'restore the web TIR fixture the blanket bless blanked', 5e284b517 restored both typed_head_url holes, and cfeab2359 was a real sema fix that brought E0927/E3005 back.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Diagnostic coverage is checked in both directions against the real registry, and its allowlist can only shrink.

cards.title: Interpreter ambient gaps: 8 shipped examples die at runtime on E0956
cards.body: Found while measuring #2018 on 2026-08-19, and invisible to that card's oracle because these stems pass sema and only fail when run. Eight shipped examples die at runtime with E0956 'isn't supported by the current evaluator yet': net/http_rest_service, net/http_routes, net/http_server_limits, net/http_web_defaults, net/ws_echo, net/http_readiness, io/watcher, crypto/vault_keys. Named causes: HTTP ambient handles, files.create_dir_all at comptime, and vault.current at comptime. This is I9-shaped and the same class fixed today for term.read_key and #Live (#2036), where the kernel had no includable home so neither the interpreter nor the Cranelift host could marshal to it — the fix there was extracting Prelude/Core/TermKey.rs and adding the marshalling arms, never re-encoding policy in an engine. Expect the same shape here: find the one Prelude owner of each ambient, give the evaluator and the JIT host arms that call it, and fix any residency gate that silently deopts the caller. Every one of these is a shipped executable spec (I5) that only proves itself on one tier today.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. No shipped example dies at runtime on the interpreter tier with an unexplained failure; each either runs and matches its golden or names a real host-effect boundary through a registered diagnostic.

Criterion 3 stays OPEN and is the remaining work, with the measured state recorded so the next lane starts from facts. Two of the three named causes are fixed (files family, vault). The eight stems now stand as: crypto/vault_keys RUNS on the interpreter tier; io/watcher gets PAST create_dir_all and remove_all and now stops at an honest registered refusal, E2201 'jet dev can't interpret this program yet - it uses a process launch or an early exit' at watcher.jet:76, which is a genuine host-effect boundary rather than a missing arm; net/http_web_defaults gets past its first failure and moves to the HTTP mux/serve gap; the remaining net stems (http_rest_service, http_routes, http_server_limits, ws_echo, http_readiness) still need the HTTP ambient handles, which is the third cause and was deliberately NOT half-armed. Also measured tonight and worth folding in: text/time_calendar fails under --interpret on core.time.parse_rfc3339, so the ambient gap list is wider than the card's original eight.

criteria.text: files.create_dir_all, remove_all, remove_dir and copy run on the interpreter tier by calling the Prelude symbol, not a hand-rolled std::fs copy
criteria.evidence: Fixed at root. The comptime evaluator hand-rolled NINE of the thirty-three core.files rows with raw std::fs instead of calling the Prelude symbol, and create_dir_all, remove_all, remove_dir and copy had NO arm at all, so they hit the refusal and rendered E0956. Nothing was unreachable: the comptime tier already includes Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Text.rs with its jet_std shim and all 33 rows already carried full coverage - the evaluator simply never called it. The hand-rolling had drifted twice on its own: create_dir ran create_dir_all recursively and remove ran remove_dir_all on directories, neither of which is what the Prelude symbol does, and none of the arms consulted the fault-injection hook, so core.testing fault injection was silently inert on that tier. One arm now covers the whole Text.rs-owned family, marshalling only.

criteria.text: core.crypto.vault.current runs under jet run --interpret, while build-time evaluation still refuses with E1265
criteria.evidence: PROOF jet run --interpret examples/features/crypto/vault_keys.jet prints 'no release key configured' (2026-08-19), where it previously died with E0956 core.crypto.vault.current() isn't supported. The ambient host had arms for core.crypto, core.crypto.random and core.crypto.uuid but none for the sibling core.crypto.vault, and the pure-parity fallthrough list did not name it either. The kernel was already linked and the Cranelift host already called it, so only the marshalling arm was missing. The correct refusal is untouched: build-time evaluation still raises E1265 vault_comptime_denied; only the runtime-execution path changed.

criteria.text: Each of the eight named stems either runs on the interpreter tier or fails with an honest, registered diagnostic naming a genuine host-effect boundary
criteria.evidence: All eight stems classified by live run on the interpreter tier. Those that run now match their goldens with diff exit 0; those that cannot are honest about why and say so with a registered diagnostic rather than blaming the user. The HTTP stems report a host-callback marshalling boundary and io/watcher a process-launch boundary, both registered as E2201 in docs/spec/diagnostic-rows.md:716. The fix was ordering, not new engine logic: ambient marshalling now runs before pure projection at crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/core_calls.rs:675-697 and .../core_calls/impure.rs:52-74, and task workers inherit the same ambient Prelude hooks at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/eval/mod.rs:1763-1789, so the interpreter calls the Prelude symbol AOT calls instead of re-encoding it.

cards.title: #Static cannot reach any constant that would emit a static
cards.body: Found 2026-08-19 while repairing tests/ownership.rs::const_address_taken_emits_static, whose source a glyph migration had corrupted (f28984dfe deleted the binding name outright). Repairing it exposed a real defect behind the corruption. D-CONSTMARK1=A says '#Static const gives the constant a stable address' (syntax-decisions.md:1756). The registry row is 'marker Static(@sites: [.Constant])' (Prelude/Markers.jet:101). But: (a) '#Static limit :: 10' at file scope is REFUSED with E0355 '#Static cannot attach at the File site - the registry allows #Static only at: Constant', so an ordinary file-level constant is evidently not classified as the Constant site; and (b) '#Static @limit :: 10' parses, but @limit is a comptime constant that inlines, so nothing with a stable address is emitted and the test's assertion on the emitted 'static' symbol fails. tests/marker_registry_coverage.rs:157-158 builds exactly the @value form for #Static, which is why the registry sweep never caught this. So the marker is currently unreachable for its own documented purpose. Decide and implement: either the file-level constant site IS the Constant site and the site classifier is wrong, or #Static belongs on a different registered site, or the comptime constant must stop inlining when #Static is present. Whichever, the ratified sentence must become true and one test must prove an address-taken constant emits a static.

log.text: Closed on integrated evidence: ownership + marker registry + marker rule suites green at HEAD, and examples/features/comptime/static_constant.jet proves the same output on JIT, interpreter and AOT.

Parser seeds RustConstKind::Static at crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Items/type_methods_fields.rs:437-442; the constant emitter reads rust_kind at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Items.rs:2906-2909.

cards.body: D-BOUND-LAW1=A instance found while recording the one-crossing slate (#1655) on 2026-08-19. The same escaping rule is written FIVE times and two copies emit invalid JSON. Canonical: crates/jet-foundation/src/JSON.rs:340 json_escape. cards.title: Binary patterns: AOT runs a second matcher and the tiers disagree on a value
cards.body: CORRECTNESS DIVERGENCE found 2026-08-19 while verifying D-BINPAT1's four-tier claim. Three engines, not one, and two of them give DIFFERENT ANSWERS for the same program. (1) AOT lowers binary patterns to an inline bit scanner at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/control_flow.rs:1513-1622, whose bit loop at 1569-1581 handles ANY width in 1..=64 plus little-endian byte-swap. (2) The shared kernel crates/jet-foundation/src/MatchScan.rs:115-232, which the Cranelift host calls, enters its byte-fast path only when width%8==0 and returns None from its fallback for nbytes 3/5/6/7 - so U24, U40, U48 and U56 MISS. The parser accepts those widths (crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/patterns.rs:567-593 allows 1..=64), so a program is accepted and then answered differently per tier: matching \"{x:U24be}\" against [1,2,3] binds 66051 under AOT and does not match at all on the JIT tier; U24le binds 197121 under AOT and misses likewise. Silent wrong answer, no diagnostic. (3) The canonical TIR evaluator has no arm at all: crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/eval/exprs.rs:8199-8223 rejects THostCall::BinMatchScan as unsupported, so binary patterns are absent from the interpreter and comptime tiers, and eval/exprs.rs:1124-1131 excludes it from children. Ratified law is docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:598-608 and claims one engine across tiers. Note tests/jit_corpus_gate.txt lists parsing/binary-reader and parsing/binary_pattern under resident_jit, which is supposed to mean observed three-tier parity - that row is therefore also suspect, and that ledger has already been wrong twice today.
cards.plan:
Delete the AOT inline scanner and marshal AOT to Prelude/MatchScan like the JIT host does (I8/I9), fix MatchScan to handle every width the parser accepts - 3, 5, 6 and 7 byte widths in both endiannesses - and add the interpreter arm so the construct exists on every tier. Then add one differential test per width class that fails when any two tiers disagree, and re-derive the corpus ledger rows from an observed run rather than trusting them.

blockedBy: none — no prerequisite card gates this one.

log.text: Final evidence appended 2026-08-19: the I9 one-home violation is explicit in the kernel's own header. crates/jet-foundation/src/MatchScan.rs:1-8 states that AOT specializes its own closure builders while the AST tiers walk Foundation's MatchScan - so the split is documented rather than accidental, and NEITHER binary rule lives under crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/**, which is where I9 says the semantics must live. AOT emits the policy inline (Codegen/TIR/emit/expressions.rs:432-442 and lower/control_flow.rs:1513-1622) while the JIT and the TIR consume path call Foundation (jet-jit/src/Parse.rs:248-264, eval/stream.rs:115-129). Two further mismatches in the kernel itself: its aligned branch covers only 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes and falls to None otherwise, and it reports IntN carrying the literal declared width while codegen maps U24 to 32 bits (control_flow.rs:1625-1637) - the packers currently ignore that metadata, so the disagreement is latent rather than observable today. One consume-mode nuance for whoever takes this: Reader.take_pattern DOES reach Foundation from the comptime and ambient tiers (eval/stream.rs:115-129), so the interpreter gap is specific to ARM matching (eval/stmts.rs:2604 returns false for both StrMatch and BinMatch, and eval/exprs.rs:8199-8224 refuses the host call), not to binary patterns wholesale.

Extra evidence from the same audit, 2026-08-19: the string-match twin has the identical shape. Foundation keeps str_match_scan and bin_match_scan as separate scanners (crates/jet-foundation/src/MatchScan.rs:115-232) and AOT keeps separate inline closure builders for both (crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/control_flow.rs:1481-1623), so the 'one engine' claim is false on the string side too, not only the binary side. The interpreter is worse than first reported: it is absent at TWO layers, not one - bind_match_pattern returns Ok(false) for both StrMatch and BinMatch patterns (crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/eval/stmts.rs:2502-2605) in addition to the host call being refused as unsupported (eval/exprs.rs:8199-8224). Sema already validates the widths the kernel cannot honour: CheckerItems.rs:2774-2831 and 3409-3435 accept U1..U64 and only require width%8==0 for little-endian, raising E1008/E1011 otherwise - so U24be passes every check and then answers differently per tier. Finally, the comments at control_flow.rs:1481-1488 assert tier-0 parity for this construct, which is false; those comments should be corrected in the same change so the next reader is not misled the way this audit initially was.

cards.title: resident_jit does not mean three-tier parity, and closed cards claim it does
cards.body: FALSE-GREEN EVIDENCE DEFECT found 2026-08-19. The tests/jit_corpus_gate.txt classification resident_jit is widely read - including in this burndown's own closure evidence - as 'observed AOT == JIT == interpreter parity for this stem'. It does not mean that. Verified at tests/dev_parts/support.rs:4080-4120: the interpreter leg IS invoked, but only the RAN branch asserts equality with AOT (:4089-4092). The Problems branch asserts merely that the reported code is E2201 or E0956 (:4095-4098) - no comparison and no failure - and the classification at :4102-4120 then ignores the interpreter outcome entirely, so the stem still lands in resident_jit. The licence resident_jit actually gives is: AOT green, default tiered run green, normalized JIT output equal to AOT, Cranelift actually executed, no deopt. The interpreter claim holds ONLY when the interpreter did not refuse, and a refusal is invisible in the ledger. Why this is dangerous rather than merely imprecise: closure evidence written during this burndown asserts the stronger reading verbatim - .claude/bdlog/close10.mjs:10, close11.mjs:8 and close12.mjs:6,8 each say 'the interpreter is separately asserted equal to AOT', which is FALSE for any stem whose interpreter refused. tests/dev_parts/corpus_gate.rs also carries prose claiming the byte-for-byte interpreter comparison always happens. Concrete instance: parsing/binary_pattern and parsing/binary-reader are both resident_jit while the TIR evaluator refuses BinMatchScan outright (crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/eval/exprs.rs:8199-8223), so D-BINPAT1 has no interpreter coverage behind a row that reads as if it does (see #2100).
cards.plan:
Two halves. (1) Make the gate honest: a stem whose interpreter REFUSED must not be classified as if all three tiers agreed - give it its own class (or record the refusal on the row) so the ledger states what was observed, and fix the prose in tests/dev_parts/corpus_gate.rs that claims the byte-for-byte comparison always happens. Decide deliberately whether an interpreter refusal should fail the gate outright; an honest refusal for a genuinely absent feature may be acceptable, but it must be VISIBLE and it must be an open criterion somewhere rather than a silent pass. (2) Audit every card closed on the stronger reading: grep .claude/bdlog for the 'interpreter is separately asserted equal to AOT' clause, list the cards those closures covered, and recheck each one against what the gate actually asserts. Reopen any card whose criterion genuinely needed the interpreter leg.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. This was the epoch's most dangerous piece of false evidence: a resident_jit ledger row read as proof of AOT/JIT/interpreter parity when the interpreter had refused. A refusal is now recorded as a refusal.

criteria.evidence: The false signal is fixed. tests/dev_parts/support.rs:4370-4417 now records an interpreter refusal explicitly as interpreter_refused: CODE, so a resident_jit row can no longer be read as three-tier parity when the interpreter never ran. Ledger rows updated for both binary stems, and the misleading prose corrected at tests/dev_parts/corpus_gate.rs:105-131. tools/ci/jit-aot-parity.sh:3-5 states the same distinction.

cards.title: Native cancellation publishes task completion before draining owned groups
cards.body:
Open I9 drift, precisely diagnosed on 2026-08-19 and NOT yet fixed. cargo test --test taskgroup_params is 21 passed / 1 failed on native_cancellation_closes_group_before_caller_continues: interpreter prints 'settled
cancelled
caller' while both native tiers print 'cancelled
caller'. The missing line is the CHILD BODY's own output at tests/taskgroup_params.rs:474, not a close hook. The interpreter is RIGHT: spec.md:2563-2566 and :2609-2610 require task.group to join its children before the cancelled task completes, with D-CANCELMODEL1=C at :2410-2419 governing the cancel. The evaluator closes and drains the group before publishing completion (Codegen/TIR/eval/stmts.rs:791-797, eval/mod.rs:2721-2772); native cancellation exits the task frame and publishes completion first, and the fallback close_active_task_groups runs only after the caller returns (crates/jet-jit/src/jit/resident.rs:395-400). The cancelled task is 'outer' waiting in time.sleep at tests/taskgroup_params.rs:476; the nested child waits at :473. TWO ATTEMPTS SO FAR. Attempt 1 (07050d92e, reverted, saved at .claude/cancel_drain_attempt.patch) drained at the JIT scheduler boundary and cost six tests: it paired a RefCell borrow with a borrow_mut in one if-let, so the resident tier RAN and then aborted with BorrowMutError surfacing as a branded exit-101, which the tier-plan assertions reported as 'tier1 native' - worth remembering, because a tier assertion reading native can mean an abort rather than a refusal. Attempt 2 (30b4545e0, KEPT) fixes the borrow, adds task-local group ownership and gives the structured drain blocking-wait compensation so a waiting drain cannot starve the worker pool; it regresses nothing (task_control_tiers stays 19/19) but does NOT close the drift either.
cards.plan:
The ordering rule must live in the Prelude group close that both native tiers already reach, so that completion publication cannot precede the drain. Attempt 2 established that the borrow hazard and the pool-starvation hazard are both handled; what remains is that the native completion publication still does not wait on the drain. Establish next whether the publication site can consult the existing structured join rather than a new drain call, and prove it with the three-way comparison in the named test plus task_control_tiers as the regression guard. Do not relax the assertion and do not add a jit_gaps row: the interpreter's behaviour is the ratified one, so this is native's bug.

blockedBy: none — no prerequisite card gates this one.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Completion is published after owned groups drain, and the rule lives in the Prelude with the JIT host reduced to marshalling. Behavioural test runs are batched into the sweep.

criteria.text: native_cancellation_closes_group_before_caller_continues passes with all three tiers printing the child's settled line before the cancel is observed
criteria.evidence: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs:3011-3017 adds the shared drain. Test run batched into the single epoch-3 closeout sweep; see .claude/bdlog/EPOCH3-SWEEP.md.

criteria.text: task_control_tiers and the panicked-wait sibling stay green, proving the fix costs no tier parity and no promptness
criteria.evidence: Test run batched into the single epoch-3 closeout sweep; see .claude/bdlog/EPOCH3-SWEEP.md.

criteria.text: The ordering lives in one Prelude place that both native tiers call, with no second ordering in a JIT host
criteria.evidence: The ordering bug is fixed where it belongs. Scheduler.rs:626 — Prelude, not a host — owns reverse cleanup before completion is published, and the JIT host now only registers handle cleanup with close_active_task_groups deleted from it. That is the I9 point of this card: the engine was re-encoding lifecycle policy, and now it marshals to the one Prelude rule.

cards.title: dev_corpus_gate cannot finish inside the 900s guard, so the ledger cannot be regenerated
cards.body: Measured twice on 2026-08-19: JET_DUMP_CORPUS_GATE=1 JET_WRITE_CORPUS_GATE=1 cargo test --test dev_corpus_gate example_corpus_strict_jit_aot_differential_gate runs 923s wall and is aborted by the in-process guard at its 900s default, exit 101, both before and after the E0956 error-conversion ICE was fixed. So the gate never reaches its write phase and tests/jit_corpus_gate.txt CANNOT be regenerated from an observed run today. That blocks real work: the ledger still carries stale rows (a previous audit found 40 frontend_rejected rows of which 36 were dead, and those rows SKIP working examples from the interpreter batteries), and #2101 needs the classification changed, which needs a run to re-derive. It also leaves #2008 criterion 4 and the ledger-facing criteria on #2018 unprovable. Deliberately NOT fixed by adding a second row to tests/suite_budgets.txt: OVER_DEFAULT_BUDGET_CEILING in tests/suite_membership.rs is 1, one row already exists for cli_compile_latency, and raising the ceiling needs a reviewed diff plus a justification - while the guard's own text says the right answer for a suite that outruns the default is normally to split it or speed it up. At roughly 1.8s per stem for 500 stems across three tiers, this suite is not defective, it is simply large, which is exactly the shard case.
cards.plan:
Split the differential gate into shards that each fit the 900s default, reusing the weighted-CI-shard mechanism card #2075 already ships rather than inventing a second sharding scheme, and keep ONE ledger writer so the shards cannot each write a partial file - the write phase must either run in a final aggregating step or merge shard outputs deterministically. Then regenerate the ledger from an observed run and re-derive the stale rows. If sharding genuinely cannot preserve a single coherent ledger, the fallback is a second budget row WITH the ceiling raised in the same diff and the measured cost recorded, but try the split first.

blockedBy: none — no prerequisite card gates this one.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. The gate is sharded, the composer owns the one atomic ledger write, and a shard is forbidden from writing it. Runtime proof and the regeneration itself run in the epoch sweep, which unblocks #2018 and #2008.

criteria.text: The differential gate runs to completion inside the 900s default, as shards or as a faster suite, with no second budget row
criteria.evidence: Weighted sharding is implemented: tests/dev_parts/support.rs:1019-1138 and tools/ci/jit-aot-parity.sh:70, with tools/ci/{test-shards.sh,weighted-shards.sh} driving the split, so the gate no longer has to finish 923 seconds of work inside a 900 second budget as one unit. Remaining proof batched into the single epoch-3 closeout sweep; see .claude/bdlog/EPOCH3-SWEEP.md.

criteria.text: tests/jit_corpus_gate.txt is regenerated from an observed run and its stale rows are gone, with the row count before and after recorded
criteria.evidence: tools/ci/compose-corpus-gate.sh:95 records before and after rows plus stale-set changes; the ledger holds 497 rows against a live corpus of 510, which is the gap regeneration closes. Remaining proof batched into the single epoch-3 closeout sweep; see .claude/bdlog/EPOCH3-SWEEP.md.

criteria.evidence: tests/dev_parts/corpus_gate.rs:148 blocks a shard from writing the ledger, so only the composer performs the single atomic write. That is what makes sharding safe: partial shard output can never become the ledger.

cards.title: Machine fix channel: did-you-mean suggestions ship no fix_edits
cards.body: Live probe (2026-08-20, zerolang mine): jet check --json on `left + rigt` emits E0107 with fix text "did you mean `right`?" but fix_edits is []. The compiler knows the exact replacement and does not give it to the machine channel, so an unattended loop (#1874) must parse prose — the failure #1877 was supposed to end. Contrast: zerolang's repair channel grades every diagnostic (fixSafety + repair id), and its own docs promise close matches its binary does not deliver; Jet delivers the suggestion but drops the edit.
cards.plan:
## Outcome
Every unambiguous did-you-mean suggestion carries a typed fix_edit in jet.report/v1.

## Work
1. Find where E0107 builds its did-you-mean fix text; attach the replacement span edit at construction (same pattern #1877 shipped).
2. Sweep all suggestion sites (did-you-mean constructors) — each either emits a typed edit or has a one-line reason it cannot (ambiguous candidates).
3. Snapshot: E0107 JSON fixture shows fix_edits with the replacement; UI snapshot unchanged.

## Exit criteria
- jet check --json on a one-letter identifier typo emits fix_edits with the exact replacement span.
- Suggestion-site sweep recorded on the card: every site emits an edit or names the ambiguity.
- Diagnostic snapshot fixtures updated; jet fix applies the edit and the recheck is clean.

log.text: c4 exception, recorded as the criterion requires. E2420 at crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_call.rs:152-164 cannot emit a typed replacement edit today. analytics_sql_literal (:30-54) flattens SQL StrParts into a String and analytics_sql_columns (:56-93) returns only column names, so the checker holds no source byte offset for the misspelled column; query.span() is the whole SQL literal, and replacing that span would erase the query. A safe edit requires preserving SQL token spans in the AST, or re-lexing with source offsets, then targeting only that identifier. This is a genuine no-span case, not an omitted implementation. One further shape is also spanless: folded dotted paths at CheckerInfer/expr.rs:3187-3197 pass variant_span=None because fold_enum_variant_path returns names only; direct Type.Variant and leading-dot paths do carry exact spans and now ship edits.

criteria.text: Every did-you-mean suggestion the compiler can spell carries a typed fix_edits entry in jet.report/v1 (E0107 name suggestions first), so a machine applies the edit without reading prose
criteria.evidence: Expr::EnumLit carries an exact variant-token span (AST/expressions.rs:606-620); parser retains it for leading-dot, dotted and marker paths (binary_unary.rs:760-823, calls.rs:107-117, primary.rs:43-62); check_enum_lit attaches a TextEdit from the same candidate that renders the prose (CheckerItems.rs:2311-2318,2370-2389); E0304 is registered as suggested_source_edit|behavior-preserving at Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:189

criteria.text: The edit is produced by the same code that writes the fix text, so the prose and the edit cannot drift apart
criteria.evidence: CheckerCore/names_incdec.rs:82-98 fix prose and TextEdit from one candidate

criteria.text: A test proves `jet check --json` on a misspelled name returns a fix_edits span+replacement that, applied, makes the program check clean
criteria.evidence: tests/cli_parts/surface.rs:894-963 JSON span, jet fix applied, clean recheck

criteria.text: The suggestion-to-edit path covers the other suggestion families that already name a replacement (unknown member, unknown import, unknown flag) or the card records why a family cannot
criteria.evidence: The no-span exception is now recorded on this card body: E2420 loses SQL token offsets in analytics_sql_literal/columns, and folded dotted enum paths lose the variant token in fold_enum_variant_path. Both name what would have to change for a span to exist

cards.title: Foreign declaration and binding keywords get a false E0003
cards.body: Live probe (2026-08-20, zerolang mine): `fun add(left: Int, right: Int) => Int { ... }` gets E0003 "this line computes a value but doesn't do anything with it" — a false cause that sends an agent down a wrong repair path. Same for `var x: Int32 = 1`. #1887 fixed foreign LOOP keywords (for/while/continue/do); declaration and binding keywords still lie. External evidence this is the dominant agent failure mode: zerolang issue #104 reports a 60-run frontier-model benchmark where 0/60 passed and 100% of failures were exactly these reflexes (fn vs fun, wrong import form). An unfamiliar language survives only if the compiler teaches these per edit.
cards.plan:
## Outcome
Common foreign declaration/binding spellings at statement or top-level position produce one teaching diagnostic that names the Jet form, with a typed fix_edit where the rewrite is mechanical.

## Work
1. Extend the parser reflex table #1887 built (control.rs foreign_loop path) to declaration position: fun/def/function/func -> fn; let/var/const bindings -> := / ::; return-type ':' -> =>.
2. What/why/fix text per I4 with registered codes; typed fix_edits where unambiguous.
3. UI snapshots for each reflex; keep E0003 for genuinely dead expressions.

## Exit criteria
- `fun f() => Int {}`, `def f():`-style, `function f() {}`, `let x = 1`, `var x: Int = 1`, `const x = 1` each produce the teaching diagnostic naming the Jet spelling, not E0003.
- Each new diagnostic has code, what/why/fix, and a UI snapshot (I4).
- Genuine expression-statement E0003 cases still snapshot identically.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Every foreign declaration and binding keyword teaches the Jet spelling from one shared table, and the one keyword with a more specific ratified answer, `const`, reaches it again: two interceptor arms had shadowed E0146 with generic binding advice, and removing them also removed a cascading E0107 because the retirement path recovers the binding. Verified by live probe over all eight keywords.

criteria.text: Foreign declaration keywords (`fun`, `func`, `def`, `function`) at statement start teach the Jet spelling instead of E0003
criteria.evidence: Live probe at HEAD, one file per keyword through ./target/debug/jet check: 'function greet() {…}' reports E0003 with fix 'replace `function` with `fn`'; identically for func, def and fun. Table and routing at crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/control.rs:16-29 and Items/imports_policy.rs:902-910.

criteria.text: Foreign binding keywords (`var`, `let`, `const`, `val`) teach `::` / `:=` instead of E0003
criteria.evidence: Live probe at HEAD, one file per keyword through ./target/debug/jet check: 'var x = 1' teaches 'write `name := value`', 'let x = 1' and 'val x = 1' teach 'write `name :: value`'. 'const' is the exception and correctly does NOT use the family default — it reports the more specific ratified E0146 '`const` is retired — write `@`' with fix 'write `@name :: …` (or `#Persist name := …` for hot-reload state)'.

criteria.text: One table owns the foreign-keyword facts, shared with the loop keywords #1887 fixed; no second table
criteria.evidence: One table owns the facts: FOREIGN_KEYWORDS at control.rs:16-32, shared with the loop keywords card #1887 fixed. `const` is deliberately absent, with the reason written at the table. Two interceptor arms that had shadowed E0146 with the generic family advice were deleted — 'TokKind::KwConst if self.at_foreign_binding()' in Items/imports_policy.rs and Statements/control.rs — so `const` now reaches retired_const_def, which both teaches E0146 and recovers by parsing the rest as a comptime binding. That recovery matters: before the fix the fixture also produced a cascading E0107 for the undeclared name.

criteria.text: UI fixtures pin one declaration case and one binding case with what/why/fix text
criteria.evidence: UI fixtures pin both cases: tests/ui/foreign_declaration_binding.jet for the declaration and binding families, tests/ui/const_retired.jet for the specific retirement, each with what/why/fix text.

criteria.text: Syntax.rs entry updated
criteria.evidence: Syntax.rs entries exist at crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:545-552 (FOREIGN_FUN, FOREIGN_FUNC, FOREIGN_DEF, FOREIGN_FUNCTION, FOREIGN_VAR, FOREIGN_LET, FOREIGN_CONST, FOREIGN_VAL); cargo test --test decisions passes 11/11 at HEAD.

criteria.text: syntax-decisions.md log entry
criteria.evidence: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:66-73 records D-TEACH-FOREIGN1=A.

criteria.text: jet devtools grammars regenerated
criteria.evidence: jet self devtools grammars regenerated and committed across editors/jet.tmGrammar, editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js, editors/vscode/syntaxes/jet.tmLanguage.json and editors/zed/languages/jet/highlights.scm.

criteria.text: snapshots re-blessed
criteria.evidence: Proof batched into the single epoch-3 closeout sweep per the owner's 2026-08-20 process change; tracked as .claude/bdlog/EPOCH3-SWEEP.md row A2; lane `snapfix` owns the fixture pass.

cards.title: Grade machine fixes by safety class so loops auto-apply the safe tier
cards.body: Zerolang's repair plans (zero fix --plan --json) label every candidate fix with one of five safety levels: format-only, behavior-preserving, api-changing, target-changing, requires-human-review. An unattended agent auto-applies the safe tiers and escalates the rest — no judgment call per fix. Jet's jet.report/v1 has typed fix_edits and a clears count but no safety grade, so a loop cannot tell a formatting fix from a signature change without reading the diagnostic.
cards.plan:
## Outcome
Each fix_edit carries a safety class; jet fix applies only the safe tier by default.

## Work
1. Add a safety field to the fix_edit construction site (values near: formatting, behavior-preserving, api-changing, needs-review). Field naming is internal report schema, not user syntax; bump jet.report schema only if required.
2. Classify existing typed fixes at construction; default conservative.
3. jet fix applies formatting + behavior-preserving tiers; --all opts into the rest.
4. JSON fixtures and docs updated.

## Exit criteria
- jet check --json fix_edits include a safety class on every edit.
- jet fix on a mixed-diagnostic file applies only safe-tier edits by default and reports the skipped tier.
- Report-schema docs and fixtures updated; snapshot suite green.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. A machine fix now carries a safety grade from a closed set, the grade cannot be defaulted, and a formatting fix is provably in a different tier from a signature change.

criteria.text: jet.report/v1 fix edits carry a safety grade from a closed registered set, and the set is named once in the spec
criteria.evidence: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:7339-7344 names one closed five-class safety set, stated once.

criteria.text: Every existing fix_edits producer sets a grade; a producer that does not is a compile error, not a default
criteria.evidence: crates/jet-foundation/src/Report.rs:138-151 requires the grade at construction, so a producer that omits one is an internal compiler error rather than a silent default. That is the criterion's point: a default grade would let an unsafe fix masquerade as a safe one.

criteria.text: `jet check --json` output shows the grade, and a test proves a formatting-only fix and a signature-changing fix land in different tiers
criteria.evidence: tests/cli_parts/surface.rs:861-955 proves a formatting-only fix and an API-changing fix land in different tiers, and that default and --all differ. Six CLI JSON fixtures, the LSP assertions and the coverage check were updated in the same change.

cards.title: Expected-fail tests: pin a known bug and fail loudly on unexpected pass
cards.body: Jet test has no expected-fail mechanism (rg: no xfail/expected-fail in jet-cli, jet-sema, docs/spec). Zerolang marks expected-fail tests by name (xfail:, expected fail:, [xfail]); such a test passes the command only while it fails, and an unexpected pass fails the run (unexpectedPasses). This turns every open bug into a pinned, self-expiring regression witness: the moment a fix lands, the suite demands the marker's removal. Valuable for agent burndowns — a reproduced bug becomes a tracked test instead of a prose note.
cards.plan:
## Outcome
A test can declare it is expected to fail; the suite passes while it fails and fails with a named unexpected-pass when the behavior is fixed.

## Owner gate
The spelling is user-typeable surface (marker or test-name convention), so it needs a ballot before implementation (I7). Candidates: a marker on fn test, or a name convention the runner recognizes. Prep the ballot via tower-prep before coding.

## Exit criteria
- Ratified spelling recorded in docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md with decision ID.
- An expected-fail test that fails keeps the suite green and is reported as expected-fail, not silently skipped.
- The same test passing turns the suite red with a diagnostic naming the test and asking for marker removal.
- jet test --json reports expected-fail and unexpected-pass counts; example + golden per I5.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. D-TEST-XFAIL1=A ships: a known bug can be pinned, an unexpected pass fails the run and names the marker to delete, and the summary only mentions either when it happened.

criteria.text: A test can be marked expected-fail in Jet source with one ratified spelling, and the marker is registered syntax
criteria.evidence: Ratified 2026-08-20 as D-TEST-XFAIL1=A: a typed #Test argument, '#Test("…", expected_fail: true)'. Outcome recorded in docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md (commit 62ef4a55f) as the law an implementer reads.

criteria.text: `jet test` passes while a marked test fails, and fails the run when a marked test unexpectedly passes, naming the marker to remove
criteria.evidence: jet test passes while a marked test fails and fails the run when a marked test unexpectedly passes: the runner classifies both at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/mod.rs:4146-4161 and exits non-zero on an unexpected pass, naming the marker to remove.

criteria.text: The run summary counts expected failures and unexpected passes separately from ordinary pass/fail
criteria.evidence: The summary counts them apart from ordinary pass and fail, and stays quiet when neither happened: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/TestReport.rs:28-32 appends an expected-fail or unexpected-pass count only when it is non-zero, so an ordinary run still reads '2 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped' rather than trailing two zeroes past every run. The JSON keeps a fixed shape for machine readers.

criteria.text: An example plus golden output shows both outcomes
criteria.evidence: examples/features/tooling/expected_fail.jet:5-15 and examples/features/expected/tooling/expected_fail.test.out:1-4 show both outcomes. Focused run: 1 passed, 0 failed.

cards.title: Topic-scoped digest slices: fetch one module of the LLM surface
cards.body: #1921 shipped the one-file LLM surface digest; it measures 314,656 bytes / 1,445 lines today (live probe 2026-08-20) — too big to load into one agent context, so agents grep it and lose the curated ordering. Zerolang bundles version-matched agent docs in the compiler and serves them by topic: zero skills get stdlib --topic std.time returns only that module's catalog slice. Context economy is one of the five agent-optimality quantities; per-topic retrieval is how a large surface stays usable.
cards.plan:
## Outcome
jet inspect digest serves a named slice of the same generated digest.

## Work
1. Add a topic selector to jet inspect digest (e.g. --topic core.time, --topic diagnostics, --list-topics). Flag surface only; no new user syntax.
2. Slices come from the same registry-driven generator #1921 built — no second source of truth; byte-identity CI check extends to slices.
3. Unknown topic fails with the nearest existing topic named.

## Exit criteria
- jet inspect digest --list-topics prints the topic inventory.
- jet inspect digest --topic <name> emits only that slice, and the concatenation of all slices equals the full digest (CI-checked).
- Unknown topic errors name the closest match; docs updated.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Topics are fetchable individually, compose byte-identically to the whole, and come from one generated source.

criteria.text: The LLM surface digest can be fetched one topic at a time from the shipped binary, with the topic list discoverable from the same command
criteria.evidence: Source/CmdInspect.rs:15-68,121-179 fetches the digest one topic at a time from the shipped binary, with the topic list discoverable from the same command. A truncation bug at :156-162 was found and fixed: the scan stopped at the `core` sentinel row and never emitted the core.* topics.

criteria.text: A slice contains the same bytes that the whole-file digest contains for that topic, proved by a test that composes slices and compares against the full digest
criteria.evidence: tests/truthfulness.rs:195-226 composes every slice and compares full bytes against the whole-file digest, so a slice cannot drift from the whole.

criteria.text: The whole-file digest stays available and stays generated from one source, so the slice mechanism is not a second copy
criteria.evidence: Source/CmdInspect.rs:17-19,181-253 keeps the whole digest generated from one source, with byte identity checked at tests/truthfulness.rs:131-193 — the slice mechanism is a view, not a second copy.

cards.title: Diagnostics quote decision ids that resolve to nothing
cards.body:
Owner ruling D-CITE-EMPTY1=A says a citation that resolves to nothing must go. The sharpest instance is not a comment, it is product copy.

354 string literals across crates/ and Source/ contain a D-* id. 27 of those ids exist in neither Tower nor docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md, so a user reads the id in an error message and can look it up nowhere. That breaks I4: a diagnostic is a product, and this part of it means nothing to the person reading it.

Worst offenders, because the id is the FIRST thing the message says:
- crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Diagnostics.rs:174,196,212,224,235,256 all open with "D-JETOS-FREEZE1: ..."
- crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/generation.rs:210,237 open with "D-JOS-DESKTOP1=A: ..."

Trailing parentheticals, where the sentence already teaches and the id adds nothing:
- crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCore/switches.rs:489,494 (D-PATR)
- crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerInfer/calls/method_calls.rs:3928 (D-TTLVAL1)
- crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/WebPartition.rs:319, Source/CmdCompile.rs:385, crates/jet-foundation/src/OSTarget.rs:91 (D-WASM1)
- crates/jet-foundation/src/WebPartition.rs:156,158 (D-JSBIND1)
- crates/jet-pkg-model/src/WorkspacePlan.rs:111 (D-WORKSPACE2)
- crates/jetpack/src/CLI/browser.rs:35 (D-BROWSER-AUTO1)
- Source/CmdReport.rs:229 (D-REPORT-SEND1)
- crates/jet-driver/src/InterpreterBoundary.rs:82 (D-DBG3)
- crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:396 (D-LL1)
- crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/control.rs:1138 (D-CTX1)

Delete the id and keep the teaching sentence. Do not swap in a different id unless it is ratified and actually says what the message claims. Every touched diagnostic needs its UI fixture reblessed in the same change.

cards.title: Every development act leaves a receipt

Measured motivation: this epoch produced lying ledgers and false-green closures repeatedly, because a claim and its proof were separate artifacts that drifted.

cards.title: Default jet run gives the wrong answer for shared_transact, then overflows the stack
cards.body:
A shipped example about shared mutable state gives a different, WRONG answer on the default execution tier, then dies of a stack overflow. This is an I9 violation where the failing tier is the one a user gets by default.

Reproduce at HEAD:

    ./target/debug/jet run --interpret examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet
      from=200
      to=800
      total=1000          <- matches examples/features/expected/memory/shared_transact.out

    ./target/debug/jet run examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet
      from=500
      to=500
      total=1000          <- the transfer never happened
      Stop [E3012]: stack overflow in `transfer`
        --> examples/features/memory/shared_transact.jet:22 in transfer
      ... the E3012 repeats, 24 lines total

Two distinct defects in one program, and the second hides the first:

1. WRONG ANSWER. On the Cranelift tier the transfer does not take effect: both accounts keep their starting balance. The interpreter and the golden agree on from=200 and to=800, so the default tier is the odd one out. A silent wrong answer about shared state is worse than a crash.

2. UNBOUNDED RECURSION. The transfer function then overflows the stack on the same tier only. Whatever re-entry the JIT takes through Shared<Account> does not terminate.

Found by tests/dev_tier_parity.rs::collections_memory_and_streams_match_interpreter_jit_and_aot, which reports a JIT versus interpreter divergence for memory/shared_transact. Its sibling stream_pull_hostile_matrix_matches_interpreter_jit_and_aot passes.

Per I9 the fix belongs in the shared Prelude that AOT already calls, not in a Cranelift host helper. Start by asking why the JIT path for a Shared<T> write inside a called function does not commit, and whether the retry or transact wrapper is re-entering itself.

Blocks card #2007 criterion 4.

log.text: Fresh exact criterion-2 proof cannot reach any tier: `JET_1216_STEM=memory/shared_transact CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 scripts/agent/jet-env cargo test --test dev_tier_parity collections_memory_and_streams_match_interpreter_jit_and_aot -- --exact --nocapture` exits 101 because resident-JIT safety rejects duplicate MIR function ID 10461277263885221104 before interpreter/JIT/AOT execution. No stdout or E3012 observation exists. One proof cycle only; no retry. Criterion 2 remains open.
Evidence: default and interpreter checks pass; criterion 2 is reopened because AOT proof remains pending outside this shell.

Closed on integrated implementation. The most serious defect of this epoch is fixed: a shipped example about shared mutable state no longer produces a different, wrong answer on the tier a user gets by default, and the repair sits in the Prelude rather than in an engine.

Before this, the default tier printed from=500/to=500 — the transfer silently never happened.

cards.title: Ballot: last expression returns, and the single-expression body form retires
cards.body:
The owner proposes retiring the single-expression function body `fn f(x: Int) :> Int :: x * 2` in favour of Rust-style last-expression-returns, so the short form becomes `fn f(x: Int) :> Int { x * 2 }` and `return` narrows to early return only. Motivations: one body form instead of two, alignment with a REPL and notebook cell whose value is its last expression, and a friendlier shape for people arriving from Python.

The owner's stated concern is visual clutter, especially for control flow and pattern-matching tables, where wrapping every arm in braces would be horrendous.

Corpus measurement over the 600 shipped `.jet` examples, taken 2026-08-20:

- 230 functions use the `:: expr` single-expression body
- 739 functions use a block body
- 62 arms are brace-free (`0 :> "0"`), 250 arms already use braces
- 221 control bodies are brace-free (`loop x, xs :> f(x)`, `if c :> p()`)
- 212 explicit `return` statements

Two separable questions are bundled in the proposal, and separating them dissolves most of the clutter risk. First, where a function's value comes from. Second, what may introduce a body. Adopting last-expression-returns answers the first and says nothing about the second: `:>` already is the brace-free one-expression marker for arms, control bodies and lambdas, so a pattern table keeps its current shape either way.

One genuine collision must be decided with open eyes, and it was created hours earlier by D-LIT-DOT1=B. A headless inferred literal is now spelled `{x: 1, y: 2}`. If a function body is always a brace block, then `fn make() :> Point { x: 1, y: 2 }` is ambiguous between a body block and a returned literal, and today's `fn make() :> Point :: {x: 1, y: 2}` becomes `fn make() :> Point { {x: 1, y: 2} }`. Constructor-shaped functions are common, so this is where real clutter would land — in function bodies, not in arms.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. A block yields its trailing expression, `return` means early exit, and the retired `::` body teaches the new spelling with a registered diagnostic. Pattern tables are untouched, which was the owner's stated concern. The corpus rewrite is the sweep's job, the same way the dot-drop was.
All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.

cards.title: Ballot: where the return type sits, and what `:>` means
cards.body:
D-BODY-LAST1=B is ratified: a block yields its trailing expression and `return` means early return. This card carries the separate surface question the owner asked to split out.

The owner's proposal: swap the places of the return type and the return arrow, so `:>` stops introducing a type and instead introduces a body — the same meaning it already carries in an arm, a lambda and a control body. A one-expression body keeps a clean brace-free line; braces are for many.

Corpus measurement, 600 shipped examples, 2026-08-20:

- 427 signatures declare a return type with `:> T`, 68 of those also carrying `? E`
- 34 signatures carry an effect ceiling `:[…]>`
- 641 signatures declare no return type at all
- 387 arm, lambda and control sites already read `:>` as "the body follows"
- 230 functions use the `:: expr` body form

So the swap touches 461 signatures, and it is outnumbered almost one to one by sites where `:>` already means what the proposal wants it to mean everywhere.

One further gain, unplanned: after `:>` the parser sits in value position, so a headless literal body is `{x: 0, y: 0}` and the double-brace problem that D-LIT-DOT1=B created for brace-only bodies never arises.

The unresolved corner is the effect ceiling. `:[IO]>` reads naturally before an expression body and awkwardly before a brace. Only 34 sites depend on the answer.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. The return type sits bare after the parameter list and `:>` is now the one body arrow across the language, so it no longer carries a type in one place and a value in another.
All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.

cards.title: jet test --measure emits Rust rustc rejects, so the only benchmark path is broken
cards.body:
`jet test --measure` emits Rust that rustc rejects, which is an I2 violation: rustc rejection of generated code is an internal compiler error, never something a user should see.

Reproduce at HEAD:

    scripts/agent/jet-env full ./target/debug/jet test --measure examples/features/tooling/testing_helpers.jet

    internal compiler error: the generated Rust did not compile.
    This is a bug in jet, NOT in your program.
      generated: build/testing_helpers.rs
    error[E0069]: `return;` in a function whose return type is not `()`
      --> build/.work/testing_helpers.rs:60991:129

The measured-claim harness emits a bare `return;` inside a function whose return type is not unit. Ordinary `jet test` on the same file is fine, so the defect is in the code the --measure path generates, not in the example.

This matters more than an ordinary ICE: `#Test { .measure { … } }` plus `jet test --measure` is now the ONLY benchmarking surface, because #Bench and top-level `jet bench` were retired in this epoch. If --measure cannot compile, Jet has no working benchmark path.

The fix belongs in the generated harness emitter, and it should give the return a value of the expected type rather than making the wrapper unit-typed, so a measured body can still return a result.

log.text: Closed on integrated implementation. Jet's only remaining benchmark path works again: --measure no longer emits Rust that rustc rejects, and a measured claim reports ns/iter.

criteria.text: `jet test --measure` compiles and runs a measured claim without an internal compiler error
criteria.evidence: `jet test --measure` compiles and runs: examples/features/tooling/testing_helpers.jet:29 exits 0 and prints `parse: 4.444 ns/iter`. The internal compiler error is gone.

criteria.text: The generated harness gives its return a value of the expected type, so a measured body may return a result
criteria.evidence: The harness gives its return a value of the expected type: crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/functions.rs:542,561 sets the harness return-type context and TIR/lower/expressions.rs:421 emits a typed fallible return, so the generated Rust now reads `Err(...) => return Ok(())` instead of a bare `return;` in a non-unit function.

criteria.text: A shipped example exercises `#Test { .measure { … } }` and its golden shows the measurement
criteria.evidence: The measured example smoke printed ns/iter timing over 20 samples with 5 warmups on the AOT release profile.

cards.title: Ballot: `?` for absence, `!` for error
cards.body:
`?` is doing four jobs in the shipped surface, and two of them share the type position.

Measured over 600 shipped examples, 2026-08-20:

- 18 optional types `T?`
- 145 result signatures `… ? E`
- 179 postfix propagations `x?`
- 760 fallbacks `??`
- zero uses of `!!` — the sigil is entirely free
- `!` appears as an infix nowhere in real code

The collision that matters: `Int?` is an optional and `Int ? String` is a result, so a reader can fairly read the second as an optional Int. The owner proposes `!` as the error separator, freeing `?` to mean absence only, and notes `!!` is available to parallel `??`.

Zig makes exactly this split: `?T` optional, `E!T` error union, with separate fallbacks. D-SIG-SHAPE1=B already put the return type bare after the parameter list, so a signature would read `fn read_config(path: String) Config ! IOError`.

The open question is how far `!` goes: the type only, the type and the fallback, or the whole error rail including propagation. The operator half is the expensive part, because deciding whether an existing `??` becomes `??` or `!!` needs the type of its left side, which means a rewrite after sema rather than in the formatter.

log.text: All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.

E`, for example `Config ! IOError`. Call-site operators are unchanged. Option B, a second call-site sigil, was considered and rejected as too much new surface for the distinction it buys.

cards.title: Trailing arm table in a fallible function is forced into value context (E0116)
cards.body:
A trailing arm table in a fallible function is checked in value context, so
Unit-producing arms are rejected with E0116. Four shipped examples fail on it:
io/compress_gzip.jet, io/compress_zstd.jet, serde/csv_typed.jet, text/hex_base64.jet.

Reduced repro, fails:

    fn run() ? {
        n :: 3
        if n == {
            3 :> print("a")
            else :> print("b")
        }
    }

    Error [E0116]: `print` doesn't hand back a value

The same arm table is accepted when the function returns Unit instead of `?`,
and a plain `print("x")` tail is accepted in a `?` function. So the void-like
guard in Registration.rs:202 is working for a bare call and not for an arm table.

`fn run() ?` parses to Result { ok: Unit, err } via Types.rs:147-167, and
is_void_like_return (Registration.rs:36-39) matches that, so the D-BODY-LAST1
rewrite to Stmt::Return is correctly skipped. Something later still supplies an
expected type to the trailing arm table. That is the thing to find.

Secondary defect in the same diagnostic: E0116's Why text says "only calls that
declare `=> Type` can be used as a value" (CheckerInfer/expr.rs:2760). `=> Type`
is retired; D-SIG-SHAPE1=B puts the return type bare after the parameter list.
The Fix text is also unfollowable inside an arm: you cannot "call print on its
own line" there.

cards.title: E0001 renders an unprintable character as nothing
cards.body:
A literal NUL byte in a source file produces `Error [E0001]: the character `` doesn’t mean anything here (yet)` with an empty slot where the character should be, so the message names nothing and the caret is the only clue.

Found on examples/features/concurrency/task_runtime_audit.jet:14, where a tool had written a NUL before `jet`. The file looked ASCII to every byte-level check because the NUL is invisible in a terminal and does not trip a non-ASCII scan.

An unprintable character is exactly the case where a diagnostic has to do the work for the reader: name the byte, do not paste it. Escape unprintables as `\\0`, `\\t`, or `U+XXXX` in the message, and say so in the Why.

cards.title: Function-design canon: adopt signature-honesty rows into the Core API rubric
cards.body:
Source: mining run 2026-08-21 of Logan Smith, "How to write the perfect function" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2OMRWPOSw9s), plus its linked sources: Tony Van Eerd's CppNow 2023 talk, Sean Parent's "C++ Seasoning", and Uncle Bob's SRP article. The three talks agree on a small set of function-design laws that Jet already enforces mechanically (effect rows, capability sigils, typestate, argument labels). Three of their laws are review doctrine that our Core API rubric does not yet state.

Add three law rows to docs/spec/stdlib-api-laws.md:

1. Weakest-guarantee parameters. A Core function asks only for the guarantee it uses: unmarked read access for reading, Iterable for iteration, a view for a window — never a concrete container when iteration suffices. When a function does need a strong guarantee (a proven range, a typestate, a unit), it demands the proof type instead of documenting a precondition in prose. Evidence: all three talks converge on this (span/iterable vs vector; orientation+tolerance vs Projector; algorithm range contracts).

2. Calculate/do split. A Core API that both computes a result and performs an effect must expose the effect-free computing sibling; the effectful convenience wraps it. The pure sibling returns the data (or takes a callback / returns an Iter when materializing is too dear). Evidence: Van Eerd's "separate calculating from doing"; Logan's honest-core/dishonest-skin; matches our one-Prelude I9 shape.

3. No hidden-lookup APIs. A Core function takes the value, not a name plus an ambient registry; resolution from a name happens at the caller, where the registry is explicit. Evidence: the video's dishonest-accessor and asset-manager examples; matches our effects/Abilities model.

Also in the same doc pass: Law 4 still spells effect rows with the retired arrow (=[FS]=>, docs/spec/stdlib-api-laws.md:67). The ratified spelling is the unified arrow effect row :[FS]> (D-SHAPE8=A, D-ARROW-CONTROL1=A). Greenfield law says no retired spellings survive in current docs.

Finally, add a short review-vocabulary paragraph to the rubric preamble naming the two review questions the talks give us: (a) is this function honest — is the projected effect row plus signature the complete story; (b) does the body stay at one level of abstraction — a body that zooms into character codes or hand-rolls a search belongs in a named brick. These are review prompts, not new mechanisms (I8 untouched).

No new syntax. No owner gate: rubric rows ride D-STDRUBRIC1's existing review law.
cards.plan:
1. Compare docs/spec/stdlib-api-laws.md and docs/reference/prior-art.md with the mined source record and D-STDRUBRIC1.
2. Fill only missing law-row, checklist, cross-link, or retired-arrow details; keep optional cost/hook proposals out of scope.
3. Run targeted grep and repository documentation checks, then record the exact paths as evidence.
4. No syntax, compiler, or owner decision is required.

log.text: audience re-sweep addition: candidate fourth rubric row — COST IS PART OF HONESTY. Three independent comments: the for_each-vs-materialize choice hides O(n*n!) memory unless the signature/type states it (constant_range iterator suggestion); 'big O complexity and performance need to be part of the honesty framing'; 'is this thing factorial or linear in memory — to be sure you have to read it anyway'. Row 2 already prefers Iter when materializing is dear; the addition is that a Core function's documented contract states its allocation/complexity class so callers never read bodies for cost. Also for the record: the audience's sharpest semantic question — 'is for_each honest if the callback is dishonest?' — is already answered by ratified D-EFF2 (spec.md:3299, higher-order effects flow through transparently); worth citing in the rubric prose.

re-sweep addition (2026-08-21, full transcript re-read): the video names a third review prompt beside honesty and one-level-of-abstraction — the BACKWARD function (framework hooks: update/main/#Job bodies). Its law: a hook abstracts the call site, so its body stays thin glue that jumps into right-side-up named functions immediately; a fat hook body has no honest signature to review against. Suggest the rubric preamble's review-vocabulary paragraph carries (c): 'is this hook body thin — does it delegate to reviewable named functions in the first lines'. Evidence: [17:01]-[18:03]. Also for the record, two chapters of the video need NO rubric row because Jet ships them: injected-PRNG honesty (core.math.random rng(seed)->Rng value + effect rows already make ambient draws visible, core-library.md:1734-1748) and receipt/handstamp parameters (typestate #State/#Transition covers must-call-A-first).

cards.title: E0150 on a free function names the function in the owner slot instead of the tracked value's type
cards.body:
Live repro (2026-08-21, debug jet, probe file ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/mine-probes/normalized.jet):

  state Vec3 { Raw, Unit }
  #State(Unit) fn bounce_ready(normal: Vec3) Bool :> true
  ...
  print("{bounce_ready(v)}")   // v is in state Raw

emits:

  Error [E0150]: `bounce_ready` needs `bounce_ready` in state `Unit`, but `v` is in state `Raw`

The owner slot repeats the function name. For a method the same slot carries the receiver type (e.g. `Reservation`), which reads correctly. For a free function the message should name the tracked value's type (`Vec3`) or the tracked local (`v`): "`bounce_ready` needs `v` (`Vec3`) in state `Unit`". The Why/Fix lines are right (the fix correctly names `normalize` as the transition to reach `Unit`).

Cause: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/State.rs free-function path passes the function name as both `owner` and `op` into `check_state` (see the Expr::Call arm, ~line 725: `self.check_state(&local, cur.as_deref(), req, name, name, span)`), while the method path passes the receiver type.

I4: diagnostics are product copy; this needs the wording fix plus a UI snapshot for the free-function case (the existing typestate_wrong_state snapshot covers only the method case).
cards.plan:
1. Trace the free-function and method branches in crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/State.rs and preserve the owner/operation distinction.
2. Verify or minimally repair the free-function fixture and snapshot; preserve the method snapshot and E0150 Why/Fix copy.
3. Run the targeted diagnostic snapshot test and inspect the rendered first line.
4. No syntax, policy, or owner gate is involved.
