cards.title: Sequence algorithm gaps: rotate/slide, gather, and sorted-list search
cards.body:
Source: Sean Parent, "C++ Seasoning" (GoingNative 2013), mined 2026-08-21. Parent's no-raw-loops catalog rests on a small set of permutation and search algorithms that make UI/reordering code loop-free: rotate (move a contiguous selection; his `slide`), double stable_partition (move a disjoint selection; his `gather`), and lower_bound/binary search over a sorted sequence.

Current Jet list surface (docs/reference/core-library.md:209): rich map/filter/sort/dedup/chunks/windows/group_by/partition/scan/fold family, but no rotate, no gather/slide equivalents, and no binary search over an already-sorted list (`is_sorted` exists; `Rank<T>` covers ordered-set membership but not positional search in a plain sorted list). `partition` exists; whether it documents stability is unverified.

Deliverable: audit whether these jobs are (a) already expressible one-liner compositions, (b) worth adding as named List methods, or (c) correctly declined per D-STR-DECLINE1-style reasoning. Any addition goes through the D-STDRUBRIC1 review and the D-ONCE-VERB1 verb table — no new syntax, no owner gate unless a naming ballot is warranted. Include the stability guarantee of `partition`/`sort` in the reference doc either way (Parent's gather depends on stable partitioning).

Agent angle: these algorithms are exactly the vocabulary that lets an agent express reorder/regroup edits without raw index loops, which is where off-by-one repair cycles come from.
cards.plan:
1. Audit crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/Collections.rs, the sort implementation, existing collection tests, and docs/reference/core-library.md for actual behavior.
2. Retain the current no-add disposition for slide/gather unless the composition audit disproves it; make lower_bound and binary_search distinct and document partition/sort stability.
3. Add only focused stability or documentation evidence needed to close the audit.
4. If a named API survives, stop for the D-ONCE-VERB1 naming/contract ballot before implementation; any later method must prove AOT and default jet run parity.

cards.title: Stored invariant facts: typestate is flow-only, ranges are numeric-only — design the missing middle
cards.body:
Source: mining run 2026-08-21 (Logan Smith's NormalizedVec3 argument plus its comment thread). The video's strongest type-design move is an invariant-bearing wrapper: a value whose construction establishes a predicate (unit length), so every consumer drops its runtime check and generic code can specialize (normalize of an already-normalized vector collapses to a no-op).

What Jet ships today (probed live):
- Flow typestate covers the pattern for locals, including free-function first parameters: state Vec3 { Raw, Unit } + #Transition(Raw, Unit) fn normalize + #State(Unit) fn bounce_ready(normal: Vec3) rejects the unnormalized call with E0150 and a fix-it naming the transition. Zero runtime cost.
- distinct + inline range refinements (D-TYPE2-REFINE1/SPELL1) cover numeric interval invariants as real types usable in fields.
- The smart-constructor pattern (private field + pub fallible constructor) works under S18 visibility.

The gap: the fact does not survive storage. crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/State.rs is explicit that when a value escapes into a field, a non-local receiver, or a loop-carried position the checker goes silent, so a struct field or list element cannot carry `Unit`; and a smart-constructor wrapper is opaque to the fact planes, so no #Pre discharge, no specialization, and no reflection row comes from it. Ranges are the only predicate that is a first-class stored fact.

Deliverable: a short design note with ballot-ready options for letting a nominal type carry a declared predicate fact that (a) is establishable only through checked constructors/transitions, (b) survives fields and containers, (c) discharges #Pre/refinement obligations at call sites, and (d) erases at runtime (I3). Candidate directions to weigh, not decide: state-carrying field types; distinct-with-fact wrappers over non-numeric carriers; registering user predicates on the D-TYPE2-PLANE1 registry. Owner gate: any surface here is new semantics — this card produces the note and ballots, not code.

Caution from the same source: the video's own cross(unit, unit) -> unit overload is mathematically false (magnitude is sin(theta); ~11 comments correct it, uploader concedes). Any fact-producing API must carry a proof obligation, not an author's assertion — which is exactly what the plane registry gives us and vibes-based newtype design does not.
cards.plan:
1. Keep docs/proposals/stored-invariant-facts.md as the design artifact and reconcile it with Facts.rs, AST/types.rs, State.rs, FlowFacts, and KnowledgeVector.
2. Preserve the ballot-ready choice set: carrier C versus A/B, checked proof producer B versus A/C, subsumption B versus A/C, and the unresolved surface home/spelling.
3. Add any missing worked examples, negative proof obligations, and acceptance evidence without implementing the fact plane.
4. Pause compiler and syntax work until the owner ratifies the exact choices; the implementation/I9 vertical slice belongs to a later card.

log.text: audience re-sweep (2026-08-21, 289 comments mined): the video's own motivating overload is FALSE and the audience proved it — top technical correction (194 likes): |cross(a,b)| = sin(angle), unit ONLY for perpendicular inputs; uploader conceded ('Yeah, you're right. Dunno where I got that idea.'). Consequences for this card's design: (1) PRESERVATION NEEDS PROOF — a stored-fact mechanism must not let an operation claim it preserves a fact by assertion; the claim needs a checked contract (an #Ensures-style postcondition under test/fuzz would have caught this — one commenter said exactly that: 'because this talk is about testability, this mistake would easily be found when testing'). (2) The audience independently derived the deeper need: most functions do NOT preserve a fact, so the valuable surface is declaring FACT-PRESERVING functions (norm-preserving map), not just fact-establishing constructors — that is this card's missing middle, now with field evidence. (3) Sealed construction: two commenters (38 and 0 likes) note inheritance-based invariant wrappers are unsound (inherited constructors/mutators bypass the invariant); Jet has no inheritance — state the immunity and keep fact-bearing construction sealed. (4) Friction ceiling: the strongest dissent (long C++ comment) — invariant types that add error paths to every math callsite are 'not a proportional response'; the beginner path must never be forced through the wrapper; fact types stay expert opt-in with magic defaults. (5) One commenter notes constructive modeling (polar angles) is a perf pessimization vs establish-then-carry — supports the carried-fact design.

cards.title: Unused-code lints: warn tier between Zig's hard error and Jet's silence
cards.body:
Mining https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dYGSPyp41vY (Zig 0.16 tutorial) surfaced both failure extremes of unused-code handling, and Jet currently sits at one of them.

Evidence:
- Zig treats unused variables and parameters as hard errors with no dial. Audience comment (4 likes): the language is "actively hostile to developers" while prototyping; the commenter left for Jai/Odin over this class of friction.
- Live Jet probe (2026-08-21): a file with an unused local binding (`unused_thing :: 42`) passes `jet check` with "ok" — Jet has zero unused-binding/import/parameter/function diagnostics. Dead code accumulates silently. For agent loops this is a real verdict-fidelity hole: a computed-but-never-used result is a frequent agent bug shape that the oracle currently never names.

Design constraint (existing mechanism only, no new policy engine):
- New L-code lint rows (unused local binding, unused parameter, unused import, unused private fn), each with registered code, severity, what/why/fix templates, and UI snapshot per I4 and docs/spec/diagnostics.md.
- Default severity Warning. Never a bare error: prototyping stays unblocked (the Zig lesson).
- Projects that want Zig-strictness promote via the existing `policy.lints.deny` surface (E1293, D-LINTPOLICY1). One mechanism, expert dial.
- The intentional-discard spelling stays silent.
- `jet fix` offers safe removal where removal is provably safe.
cards.plan:
1. Verify the existing four diagnostic rows, registry, docs, reference/liveness analysis, intentional-discard filter, and policy.lints.deny path.
2. Complete missing fixture coverage for locals, parameters, imports, private functions, used/public exemptions, and intentional discards.
3. Route only safe removal edits through the existing TextEdit/FixEngine/CLI path, with dry-run and real-fix tests guarding side effects, comptime/metadata, and public items.
4. Run lint snapshots, package default/deny tests, and focused fix tests; no owner gate or new policy engine.

- Probe: a file with an unused binding gets the lint from jet check, and jet fix removes it; intentional discard spelling stays silent

cards.title: Competitive footprint receipts: hello + minimal server RSS, startup, binary size under pinned budgets
cards.body:
Mining https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2g63UXaynaA (Prime on vercel-labs/scriptc, 120k views in 2 days) and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kr9ai5zxAcY (hardware-cost crisis): memory footprint and cold-start are the competitive axes the market is watching right now (top comment, 870 likes: "RAM x100 in cost and web devs finally discover compiled code"). scriptc leads with 2.2MB min RSS vs Node 70MB and 2.3ms TCP-ready vs Node 56ms.

Live Jet probe (2026-08-21, this machine): AOT hello = 509KB binary, 2.4MB max RSS, startup indistinguishable from an empty C binary at shell-loop resolution. Jet is already in the winning class — but the receipt exists only in one session transcript.

Deliverable: a standing, honest receipt. Two programs (hello; minimal TCP/HTTP-ready server) carrying pinned perf budgets (BinarySize, StartupTime, MemoryHighWater) per D-PERFBUDGET-BASELINE1 baseline law, checked by jet budget, with one receipt table in docs. No throughput claims (the video itself found throughput equal across runtimes on unconstrained hardware — footprint is the honest axis).

cards.title: Canonical target layout engine: byte facts for T.@layout
cards.body:
D-LAYOUT-FACTS1=B ships the layout fact surface but keeps every byte fact absent until "a canonical target layout engine" exists, and no card owns shipping that engine (board grep 2026-08-21: zero hits for it; #1690 only made the refusal honest).

Live probe today: jet inspect expand --facts layout examples/features/basics/printable.jet -> kind=default size=unknown alignment=unknown stride=unknown guarantee=physical layout unspecified byte_facts=unavailable[E0959].

Why now (video-mine evidence, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2g63UXaynaA): vercel-labs/scriptc emitted a 72-byte struct wasting 7 bytes to naive field order; the video praised the number and the AUDIENCE caught the padding by reading the C struct. In Jet that entire story is invisible: no size, no offsets, no padding fact for any type on any target. Agents optimizing memory (and the MemoryHighWater/AllocationBytes budget lens) need layout receipts, and E0959 currently refuses every question.

Scope: one canonical engine computing size/alignment/stride/field offsets per target for physical-layout-guaranteed kinds (#Layout(c), #Layout(columnar), packed scalars), honest unspecified-guarantee reporting preserved for default-layout types where rustc owns the final order; project through T.@layout, reflect().layout, jet inspect expand --facts layout, and JSON identically (one model per D-LAYOUT-FACTS1).

2. Fill only missing target plumbing or supported known-layout cases, preserving unknown/E0959 for rustc-owned default layouts.
3. Exercise T.@layout, reflection, inspect human/JSON, and the comptime example/golden on AOT and default jet run.
4. Do not invent a packed-layout marker; if the scope requires #Layout(packed), pause for the exact I7 owner syntax choice.

cards.title: Canvas devserver aborts with a stack overflow when a real browser connects
cards.body:
Reproduced twice, deterministically, on 2026-08-24.

Steps: scripts/agent/jet-env full ./target/debug/jet dev examples/features/web/ui_showcase.jet --target=web --port=7403 then load http://127.0.0.1:7403/canvas in Chromium 151 through scripts/canvas-test/driver.mjs.

Result: the devserver prints thread <unknown> has overflowed its stack / fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting and dies with exit 134 (SIGABRT, core dumped). The page renders the Canvas chrome (mode tabs Code/Split/Graph/Review, undo/redo, Graphs/Inspector rails, status bar) but shows the teaching empty state Canvas could not load - Jet source stays visible. Retry the graph projection when the server is ready, because the projection never arrives.

Not triggered by plain HTTP: GET /canvas (200, 59784 bytes), /canvas/app.js (200, 500248 bytes) and /canvas/project (200, 2856 bytes) all succeed and the server survives. Only a real browser client triggers it, so the trigger is on the live/session path the browser opens after load, not the static asset or project endpoints.

Impact: this blocks every browser-backed Canvas exit criterion in epoch 8. Multiple lanes reported real browser proof blocked and Chromium never ran; this crash is the actual cause, not lane error. The teaching empty state working correctly is what masks it in screenshots.

criteria.text: A real Chromium client loads /canvas, the graph projection arrives, and the devserver stays alive
criteria.evidence: Root cause: prepare_frontend_sources spawned raw scope threads for the parallel frontend path, so deep parser/frontend recursion ran on a default-size thread stack instead of the dedicated compiler stack. Every other compiler entry routes through jet_driver::run_compiler_work (crates/jet-driver/src/lib.rs:37), which calls CompilerStack::run_on_compiler_stack; the parallel workers bypassed it. Fix at crates/jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:87 wraps the worker loop in crate::run_compiler_work, so the parallel path uses the same one mechanism as the serial path (I8) rather than raising a stack size. This also explains why plain HTTP probes never crashed: GET /canvas, /canvas/app.js and /canvas/project do not take the multi-module parallel prepare path a real browser client triggers. Verified by reproduction: jet dev examples/features/web/ui_showcase.jet --target=web --port=7411 under jet-env full now survives a real Chromium 151 client driven through scripts/canvas-test/driver.mjs; the devserver stays ready, document.title is Jet Canvas (was 127.0.0.1), the graph projects with typed nodes and wires, and the full toolbar is live (Fit graph, Code/Split/Graph/Review, Undo, Redo, Align, Distribute, Tidy graph, Check, Run, Start debug, Search, Developer). Before the fix the same command aborted with thread has overflowed its stack / fatal runtime error, exit 134.

cards.title: env.jet cannot be entered: a package named like a provider fails E1317, and nixpkgs packages cannot realize
cards.body:
Two blockers found on 2026-08-24 while testing whether jetpack can replace the nix devshell.

1. The repository own env.jet cannot be entered at all. ./target/debug/jetpack enter -- echo hi fails with E1317 `cargo@default` puts the provider first / D-JPK-REF1 puts the package or target before @ and the source after it / Fix: write `default@cargo`. Minimal repro: an env.jet whose packages list is default.[cargo] fails, while default.[ripgrep] parses. The name cargo collides with a builtin recipe provider, so the resolver reads the package as a provider. The committed env.jet lists cargo first, so the project shell it describes is unreachable.

2. Even with a parseable env, realization stops: E1272 1 package lacks a supported Nix compatibility output / `ripgrep@default` need a pinned compatibility output. Jetpack does not invoke an installed Nix executable for package realization. So arbitrary nixpkgs packages cannot be realized without a pre-pinned fixture or Hangar output.

Also observed: jetpack doctor reports degraded, with hangar object gnome-session-e58c899b9755 has no metadata and signing key for jet could not be cryptographically checked.

Consequence: jetpack cannot currently replace nix for this repo development shell. env.jet own header already records the unmapped surface (shellHook JET_ROOT/TZDIR/clean-nix-tmp, jetDev/jetpackDev wrappers, and the whole nix develop .#full FFI/browser/graphics shell).

Before the fix this failed immediately with E1317 `cargo@default` puts the provider first, because cargo collides with a builtin recipe provider and the resolver classified the declared package as a provider. Minimal repro confirmed the class: default.[cargo] failed while default.[ripgrep] parsed. Now the same command reaches E1255 trust and names 20 packages, so the collision no longer stops resolution.

cards.title: Jetpack native Nix binary-cache admission
cards.body:
Verify standard signed .narinfo, stream, decompress and hash NARs, fetch transitive references, and atomically admit a complete closure with no nix and no curl on PATH.

Gap evidence: the NAR model accepts only Compression: none, requires FileSize == NarSize, and accepts Jet HMAC signatures only (crates/jetpack/src/Store/Nar.rs:137-187). Real cache entries use zstd and an upstream Ed25519 signature. HTTP transport shells out to curl (Store/Cache.rs:2491-2534) and the Nix endpoint shells out to nix path-info/verify/copy (Store/Cache.rs:2303-2474), which is expressly a non-answer. Nix provider results always set references: Vec::new() (Provider.rs:2551-2563), so no closure ever reaches the graph. ed25519-dalek is already a dependency (crates/jetpack/Cargo.toml:17-30).

Verified upstream floor: GET https://cache.nixos.org/nix-cache-info returns 200; a real narinfo for ripgrep-15.1.0 returns URL nar/...nar.zst, Compression: zstd, NarSize 6531256, an Ed25519 Sig, and 3 References. Plain HTTP, no nix.

See docs/audits/jetpack-native-nixpkgs-2026-08-24.md step 1.

cards.title: Signed Jetpack package catalog pipeline
cards.body:
OWNER RULING 2026-08-25: no key ceremony for now. Jetpack gets a local, unofficial package source that needs no keys and carries no signing guarantee, so the owner can use jetpack locally today. Official signed publication waits until there is a real registry.

WHAT THIS MEANS

Two trust tiers, and the difference must be visible rather than silent:

1. OFFICIAL (signed). A published catalog with an Ed25519 signature, an immutable publication point, and a client that rejects forged, stale, cross-system, duplicate and ambiguous records. This is the eventual default. Its key ceremony, publication URL, rotation procedure and operator are DEFERRED and remain owner-gated.

2. LOCAL / UNOFFICIAL (unsigned). A catalog the user generates on their own machine from published nixpkgs channel artifacts. No keys, no signature, no publication endpoint. Usable immediately. Jetpack must state plainly that records from this source are unverified.

HARD SAFETY RULES, non-negotiable:

- The unsigned tier is EXPLICIT OPT-IN. It is never the default, and a missing or invalid signature on an official source must never silently fall back to unsigned.
- Provenance is recorded. A package realized from an unsigned catalog is marked unverified in the lock and in the Hangar receipt, so a later audit can tell exactly which objects lack a signature chain.
- The signed path keeps every rejection it has today. Adding an unsigned tier must not remove or soften one check on the signed tier; the forged, stale, cross-system, duplicate and ambiguous record rejections all stay and stay tested.
- The user can see which tier is in play without reading a config file.

WHY THIS IS SAFE ENOUGH TODAY: the bytes are still content-addressed and still verified against the upstream Nix cache signature during admission. What the unsigned tier gives up is the guarantee that the NAME to STORE PATH mapping came from a trusted publisher. That is a real loss and the diagnostics must say so, not hide it.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS: the generator is `crates/jetpack/src/bin/jetpack-nix-index.rs` with `generate`, `manifest` and `verify-differential`. A working local feed lives at `target-nixfeed/feed`, currently signed by a hardcoded test key `jet-test-index-v1` whose seed is 32 bytes of the value 7. That test key must be deleted, not promoted: the unsigned tier replaces it, so no fake key remains in the tree pretending to be trust.

DEFERRED, still owner-gated, do not build: production key custody, the immutable publication base URL, the signer and rotation procedure, and the operator who regenerates the catalog when nixpkgs moves.
cards.plan:
blockedBy: none
1. Evaluate selected nixpkgs revisions off-device and collect exact derivation, output, dependency, and cache facts.
2. Convert those facts into deterministic `@jetpack` catalog records with upstream provenance.
3. Sign and publish immutable per-system targets and a retained channel manifest.
4. Verify signatures, freshness, systems, duplicates, ambiguity, and cache closure identity on the client.
5. Publish coverage and nativeization reports that distinguish native, imported, local-fallback, and missing packages.
6. Keep product resolution and realization entirely in Jetpack.

log.text: All exit criteria met with cited implementation evidence; patch integrated; workspace cargo check clean at 0 errors 0 warnings.

Owner extension 2026-08-25: the local unofficial tier must cover jetpack-native recipes too, not just nixpkgs catalog mappings, including recipes that deliver prebuilt binaries. The native provider at crates/jetpack/src/Provider/native.rs already does exactly this for omp: it fetches a GitHub release asset, verifies a pinned digest and admits it into the Hangar with no nixpkgs involved. Generalise that from one hardcoded package into a declarable local recipe.

Verdict recorded (D-VERDICT-2157-1): Jetpack gets a local unofficial package catalog that needs no keys and carries no signing guarantee, so local use works today. It is explicit opt-in and never a silent fallback from a failed signature. Packages realized through it are marked unverified in the lock and the Hangar receipt. Every rejection on the signed path stays. The hardcoded test key is deleted rather than promoted. Official signed publication, key custody, the publication URL, rotation and the operator are deferred until a real registry exists.

Owner ruled: no key ceremony now. Add a local unofficial unsigned catalog tier for immediate local use, explicit opt-in, provenance recorded as unverified, signed-path checks untouched, and delete the hardcoded test key. Official publication deferred until a real registry exists.
Planning prerequisites are explicit: blockedBy none.
Owner ruling: the public source is `jetpack`; nixpkgs is migration provenance only.

cards.title: Host-store-independent Nix closure projection
cards.body:
Run Hangar-backed Nix outputs with their exact loaders and libraries when /nix/store is absent.

The Linux overlay currently uses the host /nix/store as its lower layer and defers an exact runtime closure (crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:265-297), so a machine with no Nix store can still miss loaders and libraries even after substitution succeeds. The path also depends on host unshare, mount and sh with no equivalent elsewhere (Shell.rs:216-238,423-437).

See docs/audits/jetpack-native-nixpkgs-2026-08-24.md step 4.

cards.title: Jet repository env.jet no-Nix dogfood gate
cards.body:
The success gate the owner named: dogfooding. Cold-realize every tool this repository declares, build and test Jet with it, restart offline, and reconcile exact closure disk use on a machine with no Nix.

Measured cold-machine coverage at audit time was 0 of 20 packages in env.jet, 0 of 22 direct nixpkgs selections in devShells.default, and 0 of 48 Nix-derived selections in Linux devShells.full.

The missing acceptance sentence, quoted from the audit: with a fresh writable Hangar, empty ambient tool path, no /nix/store, no fixture directory and no nix executable, jetpack enter resolves default.[ripgrep], verifies and stores its complete signed closure, executes it, restarts offline, and reports exact disk use.

See docs/audits/jetpack-native-nixpkgs-2026-08-24.md step 5. The E1317 provider-name collision is owned separately on card #2155.

log.text: All exit criteria met with cited implementation evidence; patch integrated; workspace cargo check clean.

Lane finding, concrete and matching the owner-reported failure: the repository .jet/lock carries 1 of 20 declared packages and no source-channel pin, so locked_nix_index_key_for_project cannot build an IndexKey and realize.rs answers E1272. This is why jetpack env fails in the repo even though the index-backed path works against a generated feed.

DOGFOOD PROVEN end to end. From a Hangar deleted immediately before the run, jetpack enter resolved three real nixpkgs attrs through a signed index for pinned revision e5bdc4a4, substituted their closures natively from cache.nixos.org, admitted them into the Hangar and projected them, and the real binaries ran: ripgrep 15.2.0, jq-1.8.2, fd 10.4.2, then DOGFOOD_OK. No nix executable was invoked at any point. Five product defects were fixed to reach this: the indexed realization never wrote its lock pin; the lock channel field carries the tier realize.rs compares while the index is keyed by the nixpkgs channel name, so no lock could satisfy both; the NAR decoder handled only the hand-built fixture shape, not real closures with directories, symlinks and executable bits; two packages sharing a transitive closure object rejected the second admission as a changed immutable descriptor; and a multi-output package like jq, whose bin is a separate store object, escaped a lease scoped to a single output. Remaining for this card: coverage for all 20 repo attrs, the cargo build probe, ordered version probes and the offline repeat.

Measured dogfood progress on a wiped Hangar: a scratch project declaring #auto NixOS/nixpkgs/nixpkgs-unstable@github with ripgrep, jq and fd, pointed at a locally generated signed index feed for pinned revision e5bdc4a41d4c072fe1e3787eaa0320a384741d44, now realizes ripgrep 15.2.0 and fd 10.4.2 from cache.nixos.org with no nix installed, no fixture directory and no host store path involved in substitution. jq stops on a shared-closure-object defect (E1315, closure object sha256-21baf9f5 changed immutable descriptor), which is owned by a running lane. Three product bugs were fixed to get here: the indexed realization never wrote its lock pin; the lock channel field holds the tier that realize.rs compares while the index is keyed by the nixpkgs channel name, so no lock could satisfy both and an #auto nixpkgs source could never reach the index; and the NAR decoder handled only the hand-built fixture shape, not real closures with directories, symlinks and executable bits.

cards.title: Phase out Nix through Jetpack imports with a local fallback
cards.body: Jetpack is the package source and the final package engine. Bare refs mean `@jetpack`. The common path uses native recipes or the signed imported catalog. On a local catalog miss, Jetpack may invoke an installed Nix once against exact locks, import the closed graph, and use only Jetpack afterward. Snix and Tvix are excluded completely.
cards.plan:
1. Rename the built-in package source to `jetpack`; canonicalize bare package refs to `package@jetpack`.
2. Retire `@nixpkgs` with a teaching diagnostic that rewrites to `@jetpack` while preserving nixpkgs provenance in locks and receipts.
3. Resolve native Jetpackages, signed imported records, and verified cache closures before considering any fallback.
4. On a true miss, discover local Nix, bind it to an exact executable identity and version, and evaluate only the locked nixpkgs attr and system.
5. Convert the evaluated derivation graph into a Jetpack compatibility recipe, lock, loss report, and proof.
6. Use Jetpack for fetch, cache admission, source build, sandbox, Hangar storage, execution, rollback, and every later run.
7. Disable fallback in offline mode. Require explicit policy in CI and non-interactive runs.
8. Reject Snix and Tvix crates, source, protocols, binaries, services, and vendor copies. Use upstream Nix only as the temporary compatibility tool and differential oracle.
9. Publish migration coverage and nativeization status so the Nix-backed set can only shrink.

cards.title: Decimal literals are unusable as Float and Decimal prints its debug struct
cards.body:
Three defects found on 2026-08-24 while assessing literal type suffixes. All reproduced with target/debug/jet.

1. A decimal literal does not coerce into a Float parameter. Given fn takes(v: Float) and a call takes(3.4), sema rejects it: E0112 `takes` wants Float (a decimal number) for argument 1, but this is `Decimal`. So every Float argument at every call site must be written Float{3.4}. There is no inference from the literal to the parameter type.

2. That diagnostic does not say how to fix it. The Fix line reads: use Float (a decimal number) here. It never names the working spelling Float{3.4}, which is the only thing the user needs. I4 says a diagnostic carries what, why, and fix; this fix line is not actionable.

3. The same diagnostic is actively misleading. It describes Float as a decimal number while rejecting a value whose type is Decimal. A reader is told the argument must be a decimal number, and that their decimal number is wrong.

4. Decimal renders as its internal debug struct in string interpolation. print("dec={x}") with x :: 3.4 prints dec=Decimal { negative: false, digits: "34", scale: 1 } instead of dec=3.4. Decimal is the default type of every decimal literal, so this is the first thing a beginner sees when printing one.

cards.title: Channel policy: pinned, manual-latest, and opt-in automatic
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-08-24. Three tiers on one axis, decided by who moves the pin.

- pinned: never moves. Fully manual, as today.
- manual latest: moves only when the user runs jetpack update. This is the current #latest behaviour and stays the default meaning.
- automatic: an explicit per-package opt in. Marked packages move on their own, without the user running update.

The owner asked for a better name than #auto-latest for the third tier; the naming is owner-gated under I7 and carried by decision D-CHANNEL-AUTO1 on this card.

What exists today: channel sources declared #latest, #main or #vN.x, plus jetpack update [<source>] which re-resolves a channel and moves the lock (crates/jetpack/src/CLI/update_search_info.rs:14), and jetpack outdated which shows locked versus latest (:103). Lock movement goes through Lock::locked_source_channel (:120). So the manual tier is built; the automatic tier and the writeback are not.

Writeback, per owner: the automatic tier propagates to the declarative manifest without asking, because declaring it IS the consent. Pinned entries never propagate. Manual latest propagates when the user runs update. Nothing in the tree writes a resolved pin back into a manifest today (no write_manifest or rewrite_env path exists), so that mechanism is new work.

cards.title: oh-my-pi as the first native jetpackage
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-08-24: omp is packaged natively rather than through nixpkgs, making it the first real jetpackage and the first proof of the endgame path rather than the nixpkgs bridge.

Why omp: it releases often, and today it is installed through the NixOS user profile as /nix/store/lyjd91h440qgdmdrvi3vvglg52pgm9pa-oh-my-pi-18.0.0, so every release costs a system-config edit and rebuild. That is the concrete pain this milestone removes.

What the package looks like: the store path contains only bin/omp (a wrapper) and libexec/omp, so upstream publishes a prebuilt binary rather than buildable source. The recipe therefore tracks a release artifact, verifies its digest, and admits it to the Hangar under jetpack control. No nixpkgs attr and no nix invocation.

Open input the owner must supply: the exact upstream publication point and artifact naming (GitHub releases, npm, or another endpoint), since that determines the recipe source and the version-discovery rule for the channel tiers.

This card depends on the channel policy card for its tier marker and on the user-tools profile card for where the binary lands.

cards.title: Jetpack-owned user tools profile
cards.body:
Owner direction 2026-08-24: jetpack owns a standalone user-tools profile, independent of both this repository env.jet and the NixOS system configuration. This is where tools like omp live.

Groundwork that exists: jet tool install places binaries on ~/.jet/bin as a tools generation, jet tool list and jet tool uninstall manage them, and jet profile plan/build/switch/rollback/generations already implement source-backed, immutable, atomically activated generations with retained history.

What is missing is that this profile is not yet a first-class declarative surface with the imperative and declarative frontends the owner asked for: an imperative install or update should be recordable into a declarative profile definition, and the declarative definition should be able to realize the same profile from scratch on another machine.

Scope boundary: this is deliberately NOT the NixOS system profile. Replacing that is jetos work in epoch 9. This card gives the owner a working, jetpack-controlled tools profile without waiting for system-scope work.

log.text: Integration note from Main (2026-08-24). A first attempt rewrote crates/jetpack/src/CLI/tool.rs as a CONSUMER of a generation API that was never written, so it did not compile: 18 errors. build_tool_manifest_generation, activate_generation_locked, current_generation_locked and generation_numbers do not exist anywhere in the tree. The edit also broke module scope, since read_tool_manifest is defined at tool.rs:810 yet reported not-found at :131, which suggests a stray nesting or unbalanced brace. The attempt is preserved at .claude/parked/tool.rs.2167-attempt and tool.rs is reverted to the last good version so the tree stays green. This is the third time tonight a lane shipped a consumer ahead of its producer (see also CmdStatus on #2113 and NixIndex on #2158). What this card owes, in order: define the generation model for the user tools profile first (build, activate under a lock, query current, list numbers), then rewrite the tool verbs against it. Groundwork that already exists and should be reused rather than duplicated: jet profile plan/build/switch/rollback/generations, and jet tool install/list/uninstall over ~/.jet/bin.

cards.title: Make modular ports concise through one arithmetic policy
cards.body: Fixed-width arithmetic stays checked by default. This card chooses one expert policy system that makes modular algorithms readable without weakening division, shifts, conversions, indexing, or bounds. The Murmur3 x86_32 port is the acceptance case.
cards.plan:
1. Follow D-WRAP-SCOPE1=A. Keep exact `Int` and checked fixed-width arithmetic as the zero-annotation default.
2. Register `#Arithmetic(.Checked|.Wrapping|.Saturating)` for functions, methods, and blocks in `Syntax.rs` and marker checking.
3. Record the innermost lexical policy and its source span on each fixed-width add, subtract, multiply, negate, and power operation.
4. Keep division, remainder, shifts, conversions, indexing, slicing, bounds, and exact `Int` outside the policy.
5. Lower policy-tagged operations through existing shared functions in `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/**`. Delete no safety checks.
6. Make AOT, JIT, interpreter, comptime, and web adapters call the same Prelude operations without policy branches.
7. Reuse `Reader.read_u32_le` for endian loads. Add standard fixed-width `rotate_left` and `rotate_right` methods only if absent.
8. Project active mode and provenance through hover, semantic tokens, reflection, semindex, inspect, and diagnostics.
9. Rewrite `examples/features/ports/murmur3_x86_32/run.jet` with one visible wrapping region and the general Core helpers.
10. Update syntax law, grammars, snapshots, numeric tests, Murmur provenance, and the expected golden.
11. Run parser, sema, numeric Prelude, TIR, JIT, comptime, web, UI, and golden checks through `scripts/agent/jet-env`.
12. Run the C oracle, every Jet vector, default `jet run`, and `jet run --release`; compare exact outputs.

cards.title: Indent a block when Enter expands it
cards.body: When a user inserts a newline inside `{ ... }`, the existing content stays at the old column. Jet supports document and range formatting but does not advertise LSP on-type formatting. The fix belongs in the language server so every editor gets the same brace-aware behavior.
cards.plan:
1. Audit the existing `textDocument/onTypeFormatting` path in `Source/LSP/Server.rs`; keep one server implementation for every editor.
2. Keep newline and `}` as the advertised triggers in the LSP initialize capability.
3. Use lexer token spans and matched brace pairs in `on_type_format_edits`; never count raw brace bytes.
4. For newline, indent moved content four spaces beyond the matched opening block and align its closing brace.
5. For `}`, outdent only the matching closing-brace line and preserve all other lines.
6. Return no edit inside strings, typed text, comments, or unmatched and unsafe malformed contexts.
7. Preserve CRLF or LF, Unicode and UTF-16 positions, comments, text, and content outside the smallest changed block lines.
8. Extend unit and JSON-RPC tests for functions, arms, markers, literals, code arguments, nested blocks, partial text, and opaque regions.
9. Run focused LSP tests through `scripts/agent/jet-env cargo test` and exercise the real stdio server with two LSP clients.
10. Confirm the clients need no Jet-specific indentation extension or editor-side rewrite.

cards.title: Give durable sends one coherent lifecycle and audit model
cards.body: A durable send needs one stable identity across acceptance, attempts, delivery, restart, retention, dead letter, and cancellation. This card chooses the complete beginner statement, expert control handle, and durable receipt model.
cards.plan:
1. Follow D-SERVICE-RECEIPT2=A after the Error and Authority cutovers in #2172, #2182, and #2187.
2. Replace immediate durable-send result variants with one `Delivery` handle and one six-state lifecycle in Prelude service modules.
3. Commit the durable acceptance record before a bare `send` statement continues. Rejection remains on the shared Error route.
4. Lower a bare Delivery result to its default acceptance observation through one sema fact, not a backend special case.
5. Extend must-use flow so each bound Delivery is observed, controlled, returned, stored, or transferred on every exit path.
6. Keep Pending, Accepted, Delivering, Delivered, DeadLettered, and Cancelled as lifecycle states only.
7. Keep attempts, retention, deadline, idempotency key, duplicate status, and authority generation as typed facts.
8. Make duplicate keys return the same identity. Reject a key reused for different authority, endpoint, or message before creating work.
9. Implement wait, retry, cancel, status, receipt, and events in `Prelude/CoreLib/Top/ServiceAuthority.rs` and `Services.rs`.
10. Sign immutable snapshots with the existing Prelude HMAC-SHA-256 and authority generation key. Give events a monotonic sequence.
11. Persist identity, state, facts, signatures, and events in the existing append-only service log and replay path.
12. Update Core signatures, sema service methods, must-use analysis, TIR calls, JIT/comptime adapters, reports, JSON, examples, and docs.
13. Test acceptance, duplicate, conflict, delivery, retry, retention, expiry, cancellation, dead letter, partition, revocation, crash windows, recovery, and replay.
14. Run service Prelude, sema ownership, TIR, JIT, comptime, persistence, recovery, UI, JSON, services runtime, and golden checks.
15. Smoke the durable lifecycle on default `jet run` and AOT, then restart from the persisted log and validate the signed history.

cards.title: Return branch-table values directly and lint redundant tails
cards.body: `service_runtime.jet` returns from every branch, then returns a default after the table. A value arm table can express the same choice directly. The owner also wants a sole final expression to become the function result without repeated `return`. This card separates the safe lint from the owner-gated tail-return rule.

1. Follow D-TAIL-RETURN1=A. Amend the narrower D-BODY-LAST1 rewrite instead of adding another tail-return rule.
2. Parse and format final expressions with existing statement and expression nodes; add no new return token or branch carrier.
3. Make sema give every value-expected block an expected type and type its final expression as that block’s value.
4. Keep explicit `return` for early exit. Make statement tails and semicolon tails yield unit with focused diagnostics.
5. Remove any registration-time function-only Return synthesis that duplicates the new block-value law.
6. Lower block values and value arm tables in `crates/jet-codegen/src/TIR/lower/control_flow.rs`; engines consume TIR only.
7. Add the redundant-tail lint and source fix in the existing lint and fix registries, with comment-preserving edits.
8. Migrate `examples/features/tooling/service_runtime.jet` to exhaustive value tables with explicit `else` arms.
9. Cover functions, methods, lambdas, fallback blocks, nested blocks, loops, divergence, effects, unit, and comments.
10. Update `Syntax.rs`, syntax decisions, grammars, formatter tests, lint UI snapshots, semindex, examples, and goldens.
11. Run parser, formatter, sema, TIR, lint, fix, UI, services runtime, JIT, web, and golden checks through `scripts/agent/jet-env`.
12. Smoke `service_runtime.jet` with default `jet run` and `jet run --release`, then compare its golden output.

cards.title: Price effects vocabulary for beginner and expert use
cards.body: Beginners should not write effect or authority lists when sema can infer them. Experts need a short source boundary, first-class authority, structured policy, and complete receipts. This card chooses the source and tooling vocabulary as one system.
cards.plan:
1. Follow D-ABILITY-NAME2=A. Use `#FX` only in expert source and full role names in all beginner and operator surfaces.
2. Rename the scoped handle to `Authority`; remove `Ability`, `Abilities`, `#Abilities`, Capability, Caps, and losing source spellings.
3. Parse `#FX(Net)` and `#FX(grant: FS, Net)` through the existing scoped-authority AST and sema path.
4. Infer required effects in `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Effects.rs`; keep explicit `-[Effects]>` rows as upper-bound assertions.
5. Resolve application authority after sema and before execution. Use existing `package.jet` `authority.holds` and `authority.grants` policy.
6. In an interactive terminal, offer once, project, or deny only when declared policy leaves a required effect undecided.
7. Make project approval use the existing comment-preserving manifest editor. Never rewrite the manifest as plain text.
8. Make CI, JSON, redirected, and non-interactive runs fail with a structured policy diagnostic instead of prompting.
9. Prevent nested `#FX`, dependencies, callbacks, and passed handles from widening the outer grant or escaping their scope.
10. Project `required_effects`, `granted_effects`, `denied_effects`, and `authority` through CLI, inspect, JSON, receipts, lock provenance, and Canvas.
11. Store every approval and delegation as a source-linked receipt with scope, resource, operation, authority identity, and policy source.
12. Update `Syntax`, `Authority.rs`, sema, `EffectBudget.rs`, CLI commands, Prelude authority, TIR, JIT, comptime, web, docs, and generated surfaces.
13. Add retirement diagnostics and a repository ratchet for old names outside diagnostic fixtures and decision history.
14. Run parser, sema effects, package policy, CLI, inspect, receipts, TIR, JIT, comptime, web, Canvas, UI, grammar, and golden checks.
15. Smoke interactive once, project, deny, CI refusal, nested narrowing, handle delegation, default `jet run`, and AOT.

cards.title: Boundary law: jet owns code, jetpack owns environments
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25. THE LAW: `jet` acts on your code; `jetpack` acts on your environment. Any verb that reads or executes `.jet` source belongs to `jet`, with no exception.

This card only establishes and documents the law and deletes the verbs that violate it. The replacement shapes are separate cards (#ENVUSE, #HANGAR) and must land first where noted.

MEASURED TODAY: `jet` and `jetpack` collide on six verbs, all shipped. `jet` has 133 verbs, `jetpack` has 35.

| verb | jet today | jetpack today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| run | run a program/project | temp shell for pkg@source OR run fn run() |
| build | create a native executable | realize a package/env, don't enter |
| dev | rerun a program on file change | realize env, then run fn dev() |
| test | run tests | realize/test workspace members |
| fmt | format Jet + configured files | delegate non-Jet files to env formatter |
| hangar | inspect/maintain the package store | 12 archive sub-verbs |

DELETIONS THIS CARD OWNS (verb removed from `JETPACK_VERBS` in `crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/effects_surface.rs:538` and from the dispatch in `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/parse.rs:477`):
- `jetpack dev` (runs `fn dev()` — code)
- `jetpack test` (runs tests — code)
- `jetpack fmt` (formats source — code)
- `jetpack run` (its `fn run()` behaviour is code; its temp-shell behaviour moves to `jetpack use`)
- `jetpack build` (workspace-member build is code; the realize-without-entering half becomes `--prep`)
- `jetpack enter` (renamed `jetpack env`)
- `jet hangar` (the store is environment, not code — delete from the `jet` side)

MIGRATION COUNTS, measured with rg over docs tests examples crates Source plugins/tower/skills:
`jetpack dev` 18 occurrences/12 files; `jetpack test` 11/8; `jetpack fmt` 2/2; `jetpack build` 41/25; `jetpack run` 27/19; `jetpack enter` 26/16; `jet hangar` 60/19. Total 185 occurrences.

WHAT ABSORBS THE DELETED BEHAVIOUR: `jet test` and `jet fmt` already exist and keep their own names; they simply require being inside the env (see the acquisition card). Do NOT add env realization to `jet`.

TRAP: `jetpack fmt` today delegates non-Jet files to an env formatter. `jet fmt` must cover that. Check `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/format.rs` for what it does before deleting it, and confirm `jet fmt` reaches the same formatters when inside the env.

There is no exception. Consequently jetpack dev, jetpack test, jetpack fmt, jetpack build, jetpack run and jetpack enter are deleted, and the hangar verb is removed from the jet binary.

cards.title: jetpack env and jetpack use: the two shell verbs
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25. Replaces `jetpack enter` and the temp-shell half of `jetpack run`.

EXACT SHAPES:
```
jetpack                          # interactive TUI - RESERVED, do not build here
jetpack env                      # enter ./env.jet default module
jetpack env full                 # enter env.full (POSITIONAL, not --env)
jetpack env -- cargo build       # run in project env, exit
jetpack env -p ripgrep           # project env PLUS undeclared extras
jetpack env --prep               # materialize, do not enter
jetpack use ripgrep jq           # ad-hoc shell, ONLY those packages
jetpack use ripgrep -- rg --ver  # ephemeral run, persists nothing
jetpack use ripgrep --prep       # warm one package
```

RATIFIED SEMANTICS, each chosen against alternatives:
1. Bare `jetpack` is RESERVED for a future interactive TUI. It must NOT enter an env. Today it prints help; leave that until the TUI card exists.
2. `jetpack env <name>` takes the module name POSITIONALLY. The `--env <name>` flag stuttered (`jetpack env --env full`). Keep `--env` working on other verbs that already accept it; only `env` gains the positional.
3. `jetpack use` means EXACTLY the packages named, ALWAYS, whether or not you are inside a project. It is NOT context-sensitive. Layering onto the project env stays `jetpack env -p`.
4. `--prep` on both `env` and `use` materializes without entering. This replaces `jetpack build`. Spelled `--prep`, not `--prepare`.
5. `jetpack tool run` is DELETED. It was the arity-1 case of `jetpack use <ref> -- cmd`, which violates I8 one-mechanism. `tool` keeps only install, list, uninstall. Its ratified id `D-JPK-TOOLRUN1` is cited in code comments only and has no Tower record.
6. `jet env` becomes a documented thin FORWARD to `jetpack env`, preserving `D-ENVHOOK1=A` and the shell auto-activation hook. One implementation, two entry points. `jetpack env` is canonical; `jet env` is the beginner path.

WHERE THE CODE IS: dispatch `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/parse.rs:477`; verb list `crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/effects_surface.rs:538`; usage text `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/usage_tests.rs`; `tool run` at `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/tool.rs:360`; the `jet env` front door at `crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs:560` (ENV_ACTIONS).

TRAP: `jetpack use` must not consult `./env.jet` at all. A previous session's `use`-like path picked up the project lock and failed E1315; see the acquisition card for the RealizeScope mechanism already added for exactly this reason.

cards.title: Ref grammar: package@source#version, prefix tier deleted
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25. AMENDS the shipped ref law.

SHIPPED TODAY, per the live diagnostic from `jetpack test --help`: "Jet refs are written `name#version@source`; `#version` is optional." Additionally the tier marker is accepted in TWO positions, proven by `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/RefSpec.rs:1190` (`#auto omp@nixpkgs`, prefix) and `:1195` (`omp#auto@nixpkgs`, infix).

NEW LAW: `package@source#version`. One position only. The prefix form is deleted.

```
ripgrep@nixpkgs               unchanged
owner/repo@github             unchanged
omp@releases#auto             was: #auto omp@releases
omp@releases#v18.0.4          was: omp#v18.0.4@releases
```

The `#` slot answers "which version" and accepts either a literal version or a policy tier (`auto`, `latest`), per `D-CHANNEL-AUTO1`.

MEASURED MIGRATION SCOPE, rg over docs tests examples crates Source plugins/tower/skills:
- plain `x@source` refs: 584 occurrences across 89 files — UNCHANGED by this card, do not touch them
- prefix tier `#auto `/`#latest ` before a name: 15 occurrences, 6 files — must move
- infix version `name#ver@source`: 39 occurrences, 16 files — must move
So 54 refs change, not 584. Do NOT run a blind textual sweep over `@`.

ALSO AFFECTED, non-source: the generated index feed and lockfiles embed refs. `~/.jet/tools/manifest.json` currently records `"raw":"#auto can1357/oh-my-pi#v18.0.4@github"` — a single string carrying BOTH the deleted prefix form and an infix version. Manifest writeback in `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/tool.rs` and the lock writer in `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Lock.rs` must emit the new spelling, and an existing manifest in the old spelling must still parse or be migrated, not silently rejected.

GREENFIELD RULE: per AGENTS.md this is greenfield. Migrate every in-repo consumer in one change and delete the old parse path. Do not keep a fallback parser.

cards.title: Acquisition policy: jet never acquires, jetpack confirms downloads
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25.

THREE RULES:
1. `jet` verbs NEVER acquire anything. Run a jet verb that needs the project env while outside it and you get a coded diagnostic naming the env and the exact fix. jet does NOT auto-enter, does NOT auto-realize, and does NOT depend on jetpack at runtime for its own verbs. This keeps the boundary law absolute.
2. `jetpack env` and `jetpack use` enter SILENTLY when the closure is already fully materialized, and CONFIRM ONCE when anything must be downloaded, showing package count and total bytes. `-y`/`--yes` skips the prompt.
3. NON-INTERACTIVE (no TTY) with a download needed and no `-y` FAILS with a diagnostic naming `-y`. It must never download unprompted in CI.

EXACT SHAPES:
```
$ jetpack env            # fully cached -> enters silently
$ jetpack env            # fresh clone
  jet  env.dev needs 26 packages, 1.4 GB - continue? [Y/n]
$ jetpack env -y         # no prompt
$ jetpack env            # in CI, download needed, no -y
Error [Exxxx]: env.dev needs 26 packages (1.4 GB) and cannot prompt here
 Fix: pass -y to accept, or pre-warm with `jetpack env --prep -y`
$ jet test               # outside the env
Error [Exxxx]: this project declares env.dev; you are not inside it
 Fix: jetpack env -- jet test
```

EXISTING MACHINERY, use it rather than inventing: `-y`/`--yes` already exists and is documented as "apply a mutation plan without prompting". Trust prompting already exists with `--trust`. Byte totals are only known AFTER narinfo fetch, so the plan must be assembled from resolved closure metadata before the prompt.

RELATED FIX ALREADY LANDED, do not redo: `RealizeScope::{Project,UserProfile}` in `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/realize.rs` and `compose_env_scoped` in `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs` exist because a user-tool install was wrongly reconciled against the cwd project lock and failed E1315. Reuse that scope; do not add a second mechanism.

TRAP: a size prompt that resolves the whole closure before asking makes the cached path slower. The cached path must not pay for the plan.

Verdict recorded (D-VERDICT-2191-1): A jet verb that needs the project environment while outside it fails with a coded diagnostic and acquires nothing. jetpack env and jetpack use enter silently when the closure is already materialized and confirm once, showing package count and total bytes, when anything must be downloaded. The yes flag skips that prompt. A non-interactive run that would need a download and has no yes flag fails naming the flag, and downloads nothing.

cards.title: jetpack update: cwd-scoped, one command, plan then confirm
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25. Owner note: this becomes a critical point once jetos is in scope, so keep the scoping mechanism explicit rather than implicit.

LAW: `jetpack update` works on the CURRENT DIRECTORY context. Inside a jetpack project it updates that project. Narrowing flags select a subset; the default is everything in scope.

```
jetpack update            # everything in scope for cwd; plan, confirm once
jetpack update --deps     # project dependency pins only
jetpack update --tools    # user tools only
jetpack update <source>   # one named source (existing behaviour, keep)
jetpack update -y         # skip the prompt
```

The plan shows, per scope, what moves and to what, with package count and download size, then asks once. `-y` skips. Non-interactive without `-y` fails, consistent with the acquisition card.

EXAMPLE:
```
$ jetpack update
  jet  deps   nixpkgs-unstable  e5bdc4a4 -> 9f1c22b7   26 packages, 1.4 GB
  jet  tools  omp  18.0.4 -> 18.1.0                     676 MB
       apply? [Y/n]
```

SHIPPED TODAY: `jetpack update [<source>|tools]` refreshes project or user-tools channel pins (`crates/jetpack/src/CLI/update_search_info.rs:14`), and `jetpack outdated` lists movable refs (`:103`). Lock movement uses `Lock::locked_source_channel` (`:120`). `jetpack outdated` SURVIVES as its own verb; do not fold it into a flag.

TRAP: the tier decides whether a source may move at all. Per `D-CHANNEL-AUTO1`, a bare pin never moves, `#latest` moves on update, `#auto` moves on realization. A pinned source must report that it is pinned rather than silently doing nothing — E1352 already does this, keep it.

log.text: All exit criteria met with cited implementation evidence; patch integrated; workspace cargo check clean at 0 errors 0 warnings.

Verdict recorded (D-VERDICT-2192-1): jetpack update determines its scope from the current directory: inside a jetpack project it updates that project. Narrowing flags select dependencies only or tools only, and the default covers everything in scope. It prints one plan naming every moving source with its before and after identity, package count and download size, then applies after a single confirmation. The outdated verb survives separately.

cards.title: Detect tool drift on the next jetpack command and offer to move the pin
cards.body:
OWNER RULING 2026-08-25, reversing the earlier shim direction: there is NO shim. Installed tools keep their current projection, and jetpack notices drift the next time it runs.

WHY THE REVERSAL IS RIGHT: a shim puts jetpack in the execution path of every installed tool, so one shim bug breaks every tool at once, and it changes what `which omp` reports. Drift detection costs nothing per invocation and cannot break a tool.

MEASURED TODAY: `~/.jet/bin/omp` is a hardlink into a read-only Hangar object (verified nlink=3; deleting a hangar object gives Permission denied). A tool that tries to rewrite itself in place therefore fails with a raw permission error rather than a diagnostic. That is the user-visible defect to fix, alongside the drift offer.

WHAT TO BUILD:

1. On any jetpack command that reads the user tools profile, compare the installed tool identity against the pin recorded in `~/.jet/tools/manifest.json`. When they differ, report the drift and offer to reconcile: move the declarative pin to what is installed, or restore what is pinned. Honour `-y` for non-interactive use and never prompt without a TTY.

2. When a managed tool cannot update itself because its bytes are read-only, the failure must be a registered jetpack diagnostic that names the tool, says it is managed by jetpack, and gives the exact command to move the pin. A bare EACCES from the kernel is not acceptable.

3. Detection must be cheap. It compares recorded identity against on-disk identity; it must not resolve a closure, contact the network, or hash a 676 MB binary on every command.

EXAMPLE SHAPE:
```
$ omp update
omp: cannot write /home/you/.jet/bin/omp

$ jetpack env
  jet  omp drifted: installed 18.1.0, pinned 18.0.4
       move the pin to 18.1.0? [Y/n]
```

WHERE THE CODE IS: the tools manifest and generations under `~/.jet/tools/`, projection and linking in `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/tool.rs` around `project_install`, and `profile_install_receipt` on the cache lease.

NON-GOALS: no shim, no dispatcher, no change to what `which` reports, and no interception of another tool's process.

Verdict recorded (D-VERDICT-2193-2): There is no shim. Installed tools keep their current projection and jetpack detects drift on its next command, reporting the installed and pinned versions and offering to move the declarative pin. A managed tool that cannot rewrite itself gets a registered jetpack diagnostic naming the tool and the exact command, never a bare permission error. Detection must add no closure resolution, no network call and no full-binary hash to a normal command. Non-interactive runs never prompt.

Owner ruled: no shim. Installed tools keep their current projection and jetpack detects drift on its next command, offering to move the declarative pin. Criteria 1-6 are withdrawn as superseded; 7-12 are the ruled scope. Card is unblocked and ready to implement.

Held in deciding: three owner sub-decisions are unresolved, named in the body. Per-tool shim versus one shared dispatcher; what which reports for a shimmed tool; inline prompt versus deferred marker. Highest-risk card in this milestone because it puts jetpack in the execution path of every installed tool.

cards.title: Progress display: aggregate phase line plus per-package rows
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25. Owner's complaint, verbatim in substance: the UI showed one stage during an install and then failed; it should show multiple states like the `nh` nix helper.

MEASURED TODAY: `jetpack use` prints `resolving <pkg> …` then `✓ <pkg> <version>`. Two states, no byte progress. A real omp install took 193 seconds and a 3-package nixpkgs realization took 91 seconds, so a long silence looks like a hang.

THE REAL PIPELINE PER PACKAGE, which the display must reflect: resolve (signed index fetch + verify) -> substitute (narinfo, NAR download, signature verify, NAR decode) -> admit (write to hangar, hash check) -> project (lease + link) -> enter. Plus a closure fan-out: ripgrep alone is 3 objects.

REQUIRED SHAPE: one live aggregate line showing the current phase with counts and bytes across the whole run, plus a settled per-package row as each finishes.
```
  jet  resolving      26/26  ✓
  jet  downloading     12/48 objects   340 MB / 1.2 GB   18 MB/s
       ✓ ripgrep   15.2.0
       ✓ jq        1.8.2
  jet  admitting      31/48 objects
```

EXISTING MACHINERY, use it rather than inventing: `Output::LiveRegion`, `theme.progress_chain(phase, done, total, node, edge)` at `crates/jetpack/src/Output.rs:229` which already renders `realize 2/5 ripgrep nixpkgs`, and `RowStyle::{Ledger,Ready,Silent}`. Governed by `D-FE-CLI1`, whose acceptance term requires erasing live regions before diagnostics.

TRAPS: (1) total bytes are unknown until narinfo is fetched, so the denominator grows during the run — show it honestly, do not fake a total. (2) Must degrade cleanly with no TTY, under `NO_COLOR`, and when piped; the existing plain fallback is already tested at `Output.rs:770`. (3) 26 packages must not flood the terminal, which is why per-package rows settle rather than animate.

cards.title: Group store plumbing under the hangar verb
cards.body:
Owner-ratified in chat 2026-08-25. Reduces the non-jetos jetpack surface from 29 verbs to 24.

LAW: `hangar` is the grouping verb for everything that manipulates the store rather than your project. It absorbs today's top-level `cache`, `shared-store`, `vendor`, `clean` and `list`.

```
jetpack hangar du                          (unchanged)
jetpack hangar verify|export|import|dump|restore|copy|sign|repair|recover  (unchanged)
jetpack hangar path                        (unchanged)
jetpack hangar list                        was: jetpack list
jetpack hangar clean                       was: jetpack clean
jetpack hangar vendor [<dir>]              was: jetpack vendor
jetpack hangar cache bind|list|publish|verify|substitute    was: jetpack cache …
jetpack hangar shared install|enroll|status                 was: jetpack shared-store …
```

The word `hangar` was chosen over `store` deliberately: it is the existing ratified user-facing name for the object store, so nothing new is coined. `shared-store` becomes `hangar shared`.

WHERE THE CODE IS: verb list `crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/effects_surface.rs:538`; dispatch `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/parse.rs:477` (`cmd_hangar`, `cmd_cache`, `cmd_shared_store`, `cmd_vendor`, `cmd_clean`, `cmd_list`); usage text `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/usage_tests.rs`, which asserts specific help strings and will fail until updated.

MEASURED: `jet hangar` is mentioned 60 times across 19 files and is deleted entirely by the boundary card; do not confuse the two changes.

TRAP: `jetpack doctor` reports on hangar, cache and signing. It stays TOP-LEVEL and is not grouped — it is the first thing a stuck user runs.

cards.title: Jetpack store must not repeat the multi-agent Nix bloat: shared CAS, bounded GC, visible totals
cards.body:
OWNER DIRECTIVE 2026-08-25: multi-agent development filled a 1.8 TB disk. `/nix/store` reached 1.3 TB and a plain `nix-store --gc` freed 1.1 TiB across 1926 dead paths, with ZERO gc roots held by Jet work. Jetpack must not reproduce this failure mode, because the whole point of replacing Nix is that many agents share one set of packages.

MEASURED EVIDENCE FROM THIS SESSION, all reproducible:

1. DEDUP IS PER-HANGAR, NOT PER-MACHINE. `optimize_hangar_plan(hangar: &Path)` (`crates/jetpack/src/Store.rs:4088`), `optimize_objects_cas_pool_plan` (`:4118`), `optimize_package_tree_hardlinks` (`:4226`) and `optimize_cas_pool` (`:4397`) all take a single hangar path. Two roots holding the same package share nothing. Proof: `~/.cache/jet-omp` and `~/.cache/jet-omp2` were 1020 MB EACH for the identical `omp@releases#v18.0.4`.

2. EVERY AGENT GETS ITS OWN ROOT BY DEFAULT PRACTICE. `JETPACK_ROOT` overrides the per-user hangar (`crates/jetpack/src/Store.rs:16`, U28 / `D-JPK-NODAEMON1=A`). Lane scripts and the test suite set it per invocation, so N concurrent agents build N private stores. With 31 lanes this is catastrophic.

3. AUTO-CLEAN SILENTLY DISABLES ITSELF. Verbatim from a real dogfood run: `auto-clean skipped: Hangar object nix-index has no metadata; repair it before receipt cleanup`. ONE malformed object turns garbage collection off for the entire store, with only a dim advisory line. That is precisely how a store grows without bound.

4. NO SIZE CEILING IS ENFORCED ON THE HANGAR. `jetpack hangar du` reports honest per-object usage for ONE root and there is no cross-root total, so the bloat is invisible until the disk fills.

5. `shared-store` EXISTS BUT IS OPT-IN. `install`, `enroll`, `status` provide a multi-user broker that nobody enables by default, so the sharing mechanism is present and unused.

WHAT TO BUILD, in priority order:

A. ONE MACHINE, ONE CAS POOL. Content-addressed objects are identical by construction, so two roots must never hold two copies. Either make the per-user hangar the default for every agent, or have additional roots hardlink into a shared CAS pool instead of copying. A root must remain able to be isolated when a test genuinely needs it, but isolation must be explicit and must not be what every lane accidentally gets.

B. GC THAT CANNOT BE DISABLED BY ONE BAD OBJECT. A malformed object must be quarantined and reported, and collection must proceed for everything else. Losing GC because of one object is the defect that produced this card.

C. AN ENFORCED CEILING. A configurable maximum store footprint with a documented eviction order, so unattended agent work cannot fill a disk. The runtime rlib cache already has a bounded design to copy from.

D. VISIBLE TOTALS. `jetpack hangar du` must be able to report the whole machine, across roots, so growth is observable before it is fatal.

NON-GOALS: this card does not change the ref grammar, the verb surface, or provider behaviour.

OWNER'S ACCEPTANCE FRAME: after this sprint the owner performs ONE migration to jetpack and never touches Nix again for Jet development. A store that grows without bound fails that frame regardless of feature completeness.

log.text: All exit criteria met with cited implementation evidence; patch integrated; workspace cargo check clean at 0 errors 0 warnings.

Orchestrator fix landed: shared_cas_dir ignored JETPACK_ROOT and always resolved to the user default pool, so an isolated root pooled bytes into the global store and its inode peers sat outside the hangar being verified, which made admission refuse every object. Roots::shared_cas_dir now returns the machine pool only for the default user root and the roots own hangar cas otherwise (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Store.rs:66). This also stops tests polluting the user store. cargo test -p jetpack went 89 failing to 41.

cards.title: Jet ships three hardcoded domains nobody owns, including the default catalog endpoint
cards.body: OWNER acquired jet-lang.dev on 2026-08-25. Auditing what the tree already points at surfaced a live supply-chain exposure, independent of any marketing use.MEASURED, all currently in the shipped tree:1. crates/jetpack/src/NixIndex.rs:29 — const DEFAULT_ENDPOINT: &str = "https://index.jet.dev/nixpkgs";. This is the DEFAULT signed-catalog endpoint. The catalog maps a package name to an exact store path. Whoever controls that host controls what ripgrep resolves to for any jetpack that reaches the default. jet.dev is not owned by the project.2. crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/identity.rs:20 and :67 — HOME_URL="https://jet.dev/jetos" written into /etc/os-release on every jetos generation. Same unowned host, and it is baked into installed systems.3. Source/Publish/SBOM.rs:26 and :171 — DocumentNamespace: https://jet-lang.org/spdx/{name}-{version}-{subject}. SPDX requires the namespace to be a URI the document producer controls, precisely so a namespace cannot be forged or collided. jet-lang.org is a different registration from jet-lang.dev and is not owned either.WHY THIS IS NOT COSMETIC: the catalog endpoint is a trust boundary. Content addressing and upstream cache signature checks protect the BYTES, but the name-to-store-path mapping comes from the catalog. A hostile default endpoint hands an attacker the mapping. The SPDX namespace is weaker but still a provenance claim about a domain the project does not hold.WHAT TO DO:- Point every hardcoded host at the owned domain, or remove the default entirely so a catalog endpoint must be configured explicitly. Removing the default is the safer shape and fits the ratified local unofficial tier on card #2157: no endpoint, no key, explicit opt-in.- If a default endpoint is retained, it must be on the owned domain and the client must still verify, never trust the host.- Fix the SPDX namespace to the owned domain so the provenance claim is true.- Grep for any other unowned host in shipped strings and fix them in the same pass.`RELATED: card #2157 defers official signed publication until a real registry exists. This card is not that work. This card only stops the tree from pointing at hosts the project does not control.

cards.title: Give the Jetpack package index and binary cache real endpoints
cards.body:
Owner acquired `jet-lang.dev` 2026-08-25. The stated endgame is a jetpackages repository replacing nixpkgs, with consumed packages landing in the Hangar under jetpack control.

WHAT EXISTS: the client reads its endpoint from `config/nix-index-v1.endpoint` in the root; a generated local feed is served today by a Node script on `http://127.0.0.1:45123`. Host-owned cache mirrors already exist as a concept: the retired top-level `cache` verb, now `jetpack hangar cache bind|list|publish|verify|substitute`, binds ordered mirrors.

WHAT TO BUILD: a published package index endpoint and a published binary cache endpoint under the owned domain, plus the client configuration that makes them the defaults when the user opts into the official tier. Serving is static content: signed index targets and content-addressed objects. No dynamic service is required for a first version.

WHY THE CACHE MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE: card #2197 exists because thirty agents on one machine each stored a private copy. A project-run mirror generalises that fix from one machine to an organisation, so agents on different machines also stop re-downloading the same closure.

DEPENDS ON: the trust-root card, because an official endpoint without a verifiable key is just an unverified source with a nicer name. The local unofficial tier from #2157 remains the keyless path and must keep working.

TRAP: do not make an official endpoint the default before signing exists. A default endpoint that is fetched but not verified is worse than no default, because it looks trustworthy.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Publish the official Jetpack package index at `index.jet-lang.dev` and the binary cache at `cache.jet-lang.dev` (D-DOMAIN-LAYOUT1=A) as static signed content. Official defaults stay behind an explicit opt-in and only take effect after signature verification works. The keyless local tier (#2157) is unchanged.

## Current state
- Rust client (shipped): `crates/jetpack/src/NixIndex.rs:562-563` reads `trust/nix-index-v1.ed25519.pub` and `config/nix-index-v1.endpoint`. Its test `nix_index_resolves_documented_official_endpoint_layout` (`NixIndex.rs:3678-3679`) already resolves the documented layout at `https://index.jet-lang.dev`. The only live catalog is signed by the forgeable test key `jet-test-index-v1`, whose seed is 32 bytes of the value 7.
- Jet port: `Jetpack/Store/Source/Cache/{CacheEndpoints,CacheBindings,CachePublication}.jet` exist (the `jetpack hangar cache bind|publish|verify|substitute` mirrors). The Jet index client (`Jetpack/Nix/Source/Index/*`, #3622) is not written; `Jetpack/Nix/Source/` has no `Index/`. `Jetpack/CLI/Source/Bin/TrustRootPublisher.jet:103,155` renders the trust manifest for `keys.jet-lang.dev`.
- Trap (owner): a default endpoint that is fetched but not verified is worse than no default.

## Changes
1. Content: generate static signed index targets in the exact layout the client resolves, plus content-addressed cache objects. Serve both from object storage (no dynamic service), using `Tools/jetpack-nix-index` / `Tools/jetpack-infra` for publishing.
2. Client, in the Jet homes: `CacheEndpoints.jet` and the #3622 index client gain an explicit official-tier opt-in. They write `config/nix-index-v1.endpoint` and bind `cache.jet-lang.dev` through the existing mirror path. There is no second downloader. An unverified fetch is a registered error, never a silent trust decision.
3. Shipped-binary mirror: `crates/jetpack` gets the same opt-in until the Jetpack cutover, so users can reach it.
4. Keep the keyless local tier's behavior unchanged, and test both tiers.

## Proof
- `JETPACK_WORKER=endpoints Tools/agent/jet-env bash Jetpack/Bootstrap/check.sh --area Store --deps-from-head --tests` → `JETPACK CHECK OK (check, default run, AOT test)`, with claims for opt-in endpoint binding, unverified-fetch refusal and an unchanged keyless tier.
- `cargo test -p jetpack nix_index_resolves_documented_official_endpoint_layout` and `cargo test --test jetpack_nix_index` → pass (official layout, unverified refusal, keyless regression; these run on the shipped Rust mirror).
- Live receipt: resolve against the published index and admit one object through the published cache from a clean root. A `curl -I` of both hosts shows static object-store headers.

## Batch
batch-jetpack-store: the cache endpoints are Store-owned, and the live publication is an external step recorded on the card.

## Dependencies
- #2199 (the trust root at `keys.jet-lang.dev`). Without a verifiable key, the endpoint is only an unverified source with a nicer name.
- #3622 (the Jet index client home).
- External: DNS/TLS/static hosting and the #2157 signing ceremony.

cards.title: Distribute the Jet toolchain from an owned channel so jet self update means something
cards.body:
Owner acquired `jet-lang.dev` 2026-08-25.

WHAT EXISTS: `jet self` already manages the installation and reports the toolchain selected for a project (`jet self toolchain`, `jet self doctor`). There is no channel to update from.

WHAT TO BUILD: a published toolchain channel under the owned domain carrying versioned Jet releases per platform with digests, and the client side that resolves, verifies and installs from it. The shape already exists in the tree: the native provider fetches a GitHub release asset, verifies a pinned digest and admits it into the Hangar (`crates/jetpack/src/Provider/native.rs`). Reuse that mechanism rather than inventing a second downloader.

RELATION TO TIERS: a toolchain is the most security-sensitive artifact the project ships, so the unofficial keyless tier from #2157 must NOT be an acceptable source for it by default. Pinned digests are the minimum bar.

TRAP: a self-updating toolchain that replaces its own running binary has the same in-place rewrite problem as card #2193's tool drift. Decide the shape before implementing: stage beside, verify, then swap; never write over a running executable.

cards.title: Generate a page per diagnostic code from the registry
cards.body:
Owner acquired `jet-lang.dev` 2026-08-25. Jet has roughly nine hundred registered diagnostics, each with a code, what, why and fix text, and a UI snapshot (invariant I4). That registry is already the single source of truth, so a page per code is generated rather than authored.

This card covers generation and publication. Whether the terminal message carries the address is a separate owner decision, ballot `D-DIAG-URL1` on this card.

WHAT TO BUILD: a generator that reads the diagnostic registry and emits one page per code carrying the same what, why and fix the compiler prints, plus any worked example already present in the snapshot corpus. Pages must be regenerated from the registry, never hand-edited, so they cannot drift from the compiler.

TRAP: the pages must be generated in the same build that blesses snapshots, or they will drift. A page that contradicts the compiler is worse than no page.

log.text: Closed: tests/diagnostic_pages.rs generates 872/872 registry pages under site/dist/e/ with first-matching-snapshot worked example; exact drift+stale-page check fails the suite on hand-edit (regenerated once after lane merge, then green twice); registered in tests/suites.txt. More-line half already shipped (D-DIAG-URL1=B).

Scope confirmed by D-DIAG-URL1 outcome B: this card owns BOTH halves of the ruling. First, the diagnostic renderer appends a More line carrying the code address, for example `More: jet-lang.dev/e/E1272`, to every emitted diagnostic. Second, a page per diagnostic code is generated from the registry so that address resolves. Both halves ship together, because a link that resolves to nothing is worse than no link. Expect to re-bless every UI snapshot when the renderer changes.

Owner ratified 2026-08-25. D-DIAG-URL1 outcome B, NOT the recommended A: every diagnostic ends with its own address as a More line, for example `More: jet-lang.dev/e/E1272`. D-DOMAIN-LAYOUT1 outcome A: one host per role as subdomains of jet-lang.dev, namely index for the signed package index, cache for content-addressed objects, keys for public signing keys, dl for toolchain releases, and the bare name for the site.
All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.
